# SKIPTI Build Log

Living document. Updated after every completed phase. Every claim here is
checked against the repository state at update time; anything that cannot be
demonstrated by a file in this repo or a passing command is recorded as a gap,
not as done. Last audited: **2026-08-26**.

## 2. Decision log (chronological, newest last within each section)

### Architectural (recorded in `docs/adr/0001`–`0017`)

All seventeen ADRs listed in SPEC §18.2 were written during Phase 0, before
any application code, per GATE 0. They are the authoritative record for:
Rust core + native shells; integer minor units; local-first pluggable sync;
Automerge selection (superseded by ADR-0018); key hierarchy and
envelope wrapping; Recovery Kit; passwordless identity; never moving money;
MIT (superseded by ADR-0020: Apache-2.0); two Android flavours; light-first
design; no telemetry; guarantees; refusing the default-SMS-handler path;
notification-listener ordering; sensitive permissions only in updates;
capture-as-proposal. ADRs 0018–0026 amend or settle those decisions where
the tree and reality required it (0018 signed op-log CRDT; 0019 one app,
splitting first; 0020 Apache-2.0; 0021 hosted instance; 0022 account model;
0023 design tokens; 0024 relay persistence on SQLite; 0025 the UniFFI shell
surface; 0026 the WebAuthn relying-party ID, superseded by 0027: the RP ID is `skipti.vardrlabs.com` under the org domain, under the generalising rule that anything holding durable user credentials or data launches on its final domain).

### Implementation decisions (this repo, not covered by an ADR)

| # | Decision | Why | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| D-01 | `ParticipantId` is `[u8; 16]` UUID bytes; ordering is lexicographic byte order | Deterministic tie-breaks with zero dependencies; stable across platforms | `hlutr/mod.rs` |
| D-02 | Share-sum violations return `Err(SplitError::TotalMismatch)` instead of panicking | FFI safety: a panic across UniFFI/wasm aborts the host call; a typed error is equally hard a rejection and keeps the production assertion always-on (A-19 allows "hard runtime rejection") | `hlutr/mod.rs::compute` |
| D-03 | Percentages are basis points (`u128`, must sum to 10_000) | Float-free percentages; exact validation | `SplitSpec::Percentage` |
| D-04 | `Adjustment` semantics: `remaining = total − Σdeltas`, split equally among **all** members; deltas reference members; negative residual rejected | Preserves total deterministically without implicit redistribution surprises; matches "equal split ± per-person delta" | `hlutr/mod.rs` |
| D-05 | `Itemised`: tax and tip pooled, split equally among the union of line assignees | Matches "tax and tip apportioned"; one rounding site, deterministic | `hlutr/mod.rs` |
| D-06 | Weighted splits use largest-remainder over integer weights; leftovers to largest remainder, ties broken by ascending ID. Equal split is the weight=1 special case, which reproduces SPEC §5.5 exactly | One code path, provably deterministic | `distribute_weighted` |
| D-07 | Currency registry is a closed list (~170 codes); unlisted codes fail `Currency::parse`. Zero-decimal and three-decimal sets explicit; everything else 2 | Fail-closed beats silent defaults in a money path | `money.rs` |

| D-13 | Safety phrases derive from SHA-256 of public key material, 32 bits per word index mod 2048 | Out-of-band comparison defeats server key substitution (SPEC §3.2) | `mnemonic.rs::safety_phrase` |

| D-15 | AES-256-GCM KATs use official NIST CAVP `gcmEncryptExtIV256.rsp` vectors (Keylen=256, IVlen=96; PTlen 0 and 256), fetched from csrc.nist.gov and independently cross-verified through OpenSSL (Node `crypto`) before pinning. A third candidate row was dropped when cross-verification failed | Never trust memory for KAT material; two independent implementations must agree | `crypto_kats.rs` |
| D-16 | Nonces: 4-byte random session ‖ 8-byte BE counter, per SPEC §16.3. `Nonce::next_counter` mutates state. Uniqueness harness seals 10⁷ records asserting zero collisions (~11 s release) | Spec-mandated construction; harness caught a real bug pre-release (§5) | `lykill/aead.rs`, `tests/nonce_harness.rs` |
| D-17 | Record padding pads the length-prefixed PLAINTEXT inside the AEAD, not outside | Appending bytes after the GCM tag makes decryption impossible without a second length channel; inner padding gives the receiver exact framing while the wire size stays quantized to buckets (+28 bytes constant AEAD overhead) | `straumr/mod.rs::seal_padded` |
| D-18 | Relay `since` cursor is exclusive; omitted `since` pulls everything; duplicate push index → `409 CONFLICT`; blobs travel hex-encoded in JSON | Standard feed semantics; explicit failure beats silent accept; hex keeps JSON safe for arbitrary ciphertext | `server/src/lib.rs` |

| D-29 | Handlers read wall-clock `Instant::now()` directly; only unit tests inject time. ~~The 250 ms constant-time floor (SPEC §4.3) is NOT yet implemented anywhere~~ Superseded by D-35: the floor now exists as response middleware | Honest split: injected-time purity where logic lives | `server/src/auth.rs`, `server/src/lib.rs::response_floor` |
| D-35 | The auth surface (otp request/verify, refresh, passkeys ×4, session/revoke) sits behind **response-floor middleware**: it measures the handler pipeline's wall time and sleeps out the remainder *after* the handler returns, so no mutex is held while waiting. Production constant: fixed 250 ms, deliberately not configurable — an anti-enumeration control operators could dial down would be a control in name only. Tests inject their own floor via `new_shared_state_with_auth_floor` (existing suites run at zero to keep the gate fast). Sync surface, devices list and health stay outside: bearer-gated or static, no existence oracle, and 250 ms per sync call would be pure harm. tokio gained its `time` feature (flag on an existing dependency, not a new one) | SPEC §4.3 mandates a 250 ms floor so timing cannot become an account-existence oracle; A-10 requires known-vs-unknown to differ below noise with both above the floor. `passkey authenticate/start` was a live contrast: unknown accounts answered after a hashmap miss while registered accounts paid for challenge building | `server/src/lib.rs::response_floor`, `server/tests/timing_http.rs` |
| D-36 | Escrow is real end-to-end (SPEC §3.3, adversarial test A-20). Core already had `lykill::escrow` (passphrase → Argon2id KEK → HKDF `"skipti/v1/escrow"` domain → AEAD-sealed MK) — the log's "does not exist" claim was wrong; reconciled. Added here: canonical wire packing (`to_wire`/`from_wire`: 16B salt ‖ 4B session ‖ 8B BE counter ‖ ct) so the server carries opaque bytes only, and `PUT/POST + GET /v1/auth/escrow` behind the bearer gate: one blob per subject, hex + 4096-byte cap as the only validation, upsert on passphrase change (KEK re-wrap only, §3.5), GET answers solely about the caller. Proof: exfiltrated blob fails four wrong passphrases and byte-flip tamper, opens for the holder; canary check that neither MK nor passphrase appears in stored bytes | A-20 ("blob exfiltrated from the server is useless without the passphrase") had no server to exfiltrate from. The escrow suite costs ~8 s because every unwrap runs Argon2id at production parameters — SPEC forbids lowering them for test speed | `core/src/lykill/mod.rs`, `server/src/lib.rs`, `server/tests/escrow_http.rs` |
| D-37 | Group-key rotation with re-wrap lives in core as `lykill::rotate_group_key`: the initiator mints epoch n+1's key (fresh 32 random bytes, zeroized staging) and wraps it for exactly the surviving devices at the new epoch; the revoked device appears in **no** envelope, so no current key exists for it anywhere it can reach — even a stolen copy of every envelope requires a survivor's X25519 private key to open, and its stale epoch-0 key cannot read epoch-1 data (different key + epoch-bound AAD). Refuses zero survivors and epoch overflow; fresh randomness per call. Member removal is the same operation with a different survivor set. Proof spans both halves of A-12: server rejection (D-34) plus crypto non-recovery over the real HTTP surface in `a12_revocation.rs` | SPEC §6 mandates rotation on member removal and device revocation; A-12's "holds no current group key" half was the last open GATE 4 item. Rotation is client-core protocol work by design — the server stays an opaque transport (D-28) | `core/src/lykill/mod.rs`, `server/tests/a12_revocation.rs` |
| D-38 | The duplicate rotation implementations are consolidated: `lykill::rotate_group_key` is the single crypto primitive (signature narrowed from `&DeviceKeys` to the agreement secret it actually uses); `straumr::GroupKeyState::rotate` — now a method, not a free fn — delegates to it and repacks into the persisted envelope map. Historical `(device_id, pubkey)` argument order kept at the state layer | ADR-0018 deferred this consolidation to the skrin session because which shape survives is a persistence question; skrin persists `GroupKeyState`, so the state type owns the shape and lykill owns the crypto | `core/src/lykill/mod.rs`, `core/src/straumr/mod.rs` |
| D-39 | **skrin** (`core/src/skrin/`, native-only): SQLCipher vault via rusqlite 0.40 `bundled-sqlcipher` holding sealed records (header columns indexed, payload opaque), HLC state, group key state with atomic rotate-replace, this device's signing seed + agreement scalar, and sync cursors in kv. Database key (32B random) lives only behind a **Keystore trait** — iOS Keychain / Android Keystore / web implement it in Phase 7; CI proves the store with MemoryKeystore (in-memory, zeroized). The trait has no export-to-disk path, so A-17's "keys not present in backup" holds by construction headlessly. Schema versioned from row one: PRAGMA user_version + transactional ordered migrations; newer vaults refuse to open rather than downgrade; record payloads stay opaque blobs so ADR-0018's tripwire shapes need no destructive migration. Wrong key is `WrongKey`, never a silent re-key | Phase 2's last unticked row; ADR-0018 made schema versioning a precondition. Dependency justification per rule 4 lives in the commit message (rusqlite/Zetetic, MIT, core deps 9→10 of 30) | `core/src/skrin/mod.rs`, `core/src/skrin/schema_v1.sql` |
| D-30 | Passkeys use `webauthn-rs` 0.5 rather than a hand-rolled CTAP2/COSE verifier. Challenge state is server-held, keyed by a random 16-byte id, single-use (removed on finish) with a 120 s TTL swept lazily on access | WebAuthn verification is attestation, COSE key and signature parsing — exactly the code that should not be written from scratch in a money app. New-dependency justification per §15 standing rules | `server/src/passkey.rs` |
| D-31 | `SessionManager::create_session` takes the subject as a **constructor argument**; there is no API that mints an unattributed session. `subject(family_id, now)` returns `None` for revoked, expired, and reuse-killed families | SPEC §4.3 requires every session to appear in the device list, which is unbuildable on families that do not know their owner. `passkey_auth_finish` was verifying an identity and discarding it (caught as an unused-variable lint); making the subject non-optional at the type level means that class of bug cannot recur | `server/src/auth.rs` |
| D-32 | Passkey happy-path proof uses `webauthn-authenticator-rs` =0.5.5 (dev-dependency only): a `SoftPasskey` drives a real registration and assertion through all four `/v1/auth/passkey/*` routes; the test asserts `subject()` on the minted family equals the identifier whose credential signed. §15 justification: it produces real COSE keys, attestation objects and signatures so the server's full verification path executes in CI; it replaces hand-rolling an authenticator emulator (CBOR attestation encoding, ECDSA signing) in tests — the same class of code D-30 refused to write. Same kanidm project as `webauthn-rs`, lockstep releases, pinned to the locked verifier's 0.5.5 so proto types unify (Cargo.lock: webauthn-rs/core/proto all 0.5.5). Caveat kept honest: `SoftPasskey::new(true)` asserts the user-verified bit without a biometric — signature material is fully real, UV is claimed | The path from `finish_passkey_authentication` onward had never executed successfully; without this test "passkeys work" was an unproven claim sitting under GATE 4 | `server/tests/passkey_http.rs` |
| D-33 | Every session mints a 32-byte **access token** (15 min TTL, SPEC §4.3) alongside its rotating refresh token; `/v1/logs/*` and `/v1/envelopes/*` sit behind `Authorization: Bearer` middleware. At most one access token per family is outstanding; rotation kills its predecessor; revocation and reuse-detection sweep the grant map; `validate_access` re-checks family liveness rather than trusting the map. Rejection is uniform `401 {}` for every failure mode (D-27 shape); auth routes and `/` stay open. Token lookup is a keyed table probe, not a comparison loop — sound at 256-bit entropy, unlike the OTP codes where constant-time comparison remains mandatory | Until now anyone could push ciphertext into anyone's sync log anonymously, and A-12's "device revoked, then attempts sync" had nothing to reject with. Access tokens were also simply missing from the §4.3 model the server implemented | `server/src/auth.rs`, `server/src/lib.rs::require_bearer`, `server/tests/bearer_http.rs` |
| D-34 | The device list is **session-derived**: every family is a device entry with a client-chosen label (clamped 64 chars, `"unnamed"` fallback, optional on both sign-in paths). `GET /v1/devices` sits behind the bearer gate and returns only the authenticated subject's rows, marked `current` for the calling session — scoping runs inside `SessionManager` against one subject, so cross-account enumeration has no surface. Revocation (`POST /v1/auth/session/revoke`) moved **inside** the gate and is owner-scoped via `revoke_device_as`: unknown ids and foreign ids collapse to one rejection; success still kills refresh + access tokens + attribution (D-33). `require_bearer` vouches subject + family into request extensions so gated handlers never re-parse credentials | §4.3 requires every session to appear in the device list with revocation; the old revoke endpoint accepted unauthenticated requests from anyone for any family id. This is also the server-side core of A-12: revoked devices fail sync, cannot mint tokens, and attribute to nobody | `server/src/auth.rs`, `server/src/lib.rs`, `server/tests/bearer_http.rs` |
| D-40 | **Relay vault implementation**: SQLite (WAL, `synchronous=FULL`) via rusqlite behind the `RelayPersistence` trait — ADR-0024 chose the engine, this row records the shape. Write-through after every persisted in-memory mutation; a persistence failure fails the request (5xx) rather than pretending success. Semantics per category: logs row-per-push; sessions and envelopes full-set replace (snapshot per mutation); escrow and passkeys upsert. Expiries cross the boundary as wall-clock millis remaining (`Instant` has no epoch meaning) and round-trip through checked u64↔i64 helpers — SQLite has no unsigned integers, and a wrapped log index would corrupt log ordering silently. Expired families are skipped at BOTH export and load, so a restart cannot resurrect a dead family. OTP codes and WebAuthn challenge state deliberately have no write path at all. Proof: `persist_restart.rs` drops the whole process state, reopens from the same file, and asserts each MUST-persist category byte-identical plus the not-persisted set gone; refresh-family rotation/reuse-detection survives intact across the restart (D-26's stolen-token window stays closed). The suite caught one real defect on its first run: `envelope_push` was memory-only — `replace_group_envelopes` existed but nothing called it (incident §5.8), fixed here | ADR-0021 made restart survival a hard precondition of any real user; a lost escrow blob is a lost Master Key recovery path. 378 lines of storage code with zero reopen evidence claimed more than the tree demonstrated | `server/src/persist.rs`, write-through call sites in `server/src/lib.rs`, `server/tests/persist_restart.rs` |
| D-41 | **Subject-owned sync surface implemented** (ADR-0022's design, now load-bearing). New `registry.rs`: identifier → opaque 16-byte random `subject_id`, derived at first authentication and held server-side; sync device bindings (device_id → subject_id) that are idempotent for the owner and refuse foreign claims forever. Sessions carry the subject_id (the raw identifier never reaches a handler or response); `SessionCreated` returns the caller's own namespace so they can address their bucket without leaking anything enumerable. Bucket ownership is the namespace by construction: `/v1/logs/{account}` requires `account == ctx.subject`, one uniform rejection otherwise — not claimed, transferred or raced. Group membership derives from the envelope set through device bindings; first push creates (sender must be among recipients), members add members, `POST /v1/envelopes/{group}/replace` swaps the set wholesale at rotation so D-37 revocation ends READ access too, and envelope GETs are per-recipient filtered (calling device when declared, subject fleet otherwise). Registry persists in vault schema v2 (`r_subjects`, `r_devices`; v1 files migrate in place, verified). Escrow confirmed compliant with zero code change — it keys on `ctx.subject`, which now IS the subject_id. | D-103 | **The unauthenticated auth surface gets bounded memory, a backoff that cannot collapse, and a cursor that cannot wrap.** Three defects found in the same audit pass as D-102, all reachable from the network. (1) **`OtpManager` grew without bound.** Both `issue` and `verify` did `entry(identifier).or_default()` on a caller-chosen string, nothing pruned the map, and the per-identifier rate limit NEVER engages when every request names a fresh identifier — so `/v1/auth/otp/request` was unauthenticated unbounded memory growth at full concurrency (the 250 ms floor sleeps without holding the lock, so it throttles nothing). Now: identifiers longer than 320 octets (RFC 5321) are never tracked, inert records — no unexpired code, no live lockout, no request inside the hour — are swept, and a hard ceiling REFUSES a new identifier rather than evicting an existing one, so a flood cannot displace a victim's lockout or pending code. (2) **The lockout backoff collapsed at the shift boundary.** `1 << (failed_attempts - 5)` panics in debug and MASKS in release: at 37 failures the exponent is 32, `1u32 << 32` becomes `1 << 0`, and the penalty falls from sixteen hours back to its fifteen-minute base — the attacker rewarded for persisting. Exponent clamped at six doublings. | D-105 | **ADR-0032: the relay gets rate limiting that learns no address — two layers, and the refusals are the load-bearing part.** D-103's open fork, taken. Every existing limiter keys on the caller-supplied IDENTIFIER, so naming a fresh one each request is limited by nothing; D-103 bounded how much anonymous state can EXIST (a right answer), this bounds how fast it can be CREATED (a trade). The trade is sharp because ADR-0021 seats this project at **A3** in its own threat model and THREAT_MODEL publishes 'No IP logging' unqualified — and every conventional per-client limiter wants the one input that must never enter the relay. **The unlock was reading the promise precisely**, now written into THREAT_MODEL so nobody re-derives it: the address is unavoidably present IN TRANSIT (the kernel reads it off every packet, Caddy reads it to answer) and no hosted service can avoid that; what is forbidden is RETENTION and CORRELATION. The loose reading forbids rate limiting outright and the loose reading is wrong. **Layer 1** — `iptables -m hashlimit` on new connections to 443, in `deploy/skipti-connection-limit.sh` rather than as a doc snippet, because the constraint a copied command loses is the one that matters: these rules must NEVER carry `-j LOG`, and `verify` FAILS if any LOG target exists in the chain. Placed BELOW Caddy and the relay on purpose — the component that already had the address by physical necessity is the one that uses it, and nothing above ever gains it. Kernel table is fixed-size, LRU-evicted, expiring, written nowhere. Honest limit stated in the script header: it counts CONNECTIONS, not requests, so keep-alive defeats it — which is exactly why there is a layer 2. **Layer 2** — a global integer token bucket in `OtpManager` (10/s, burst 60) gating admission of NEVER-SEEN identifiers. The property that makes it right here is that it takes **no client key of any kind** — nothing to hash, salt, retain or leak, so it cannot weaken §2.6 even in principle. Charged only where new state is about to be created and only after D-103's cap has already allowed it, so anyone already tracked (a live code, an active lockout) never touches it: the failure mode is 'the queue is long', never 'your account stopped working'. **REFUSED AND RECORDED, with reasons:** (1) a per-address bucket inside the relay keyed on a salted rotating hash — arguably within the promise, refused anyway because it puts the address INTO the component the threat model calls the adversary and needs `X-Forwarded-For` trust to get it, and 'arguably' is not the standard §2.6 is held to; (2) Cloudflare proxying — reverses DEPLOY-ORACLE §5's recorded DNS-only decision and adds a party to §2.6's table; (3) a custom `xcaddy` build for `caddy-ratelimit` — loses the apt upgrade path for the TLS terminator, and an unpatched TLS terminator is a worse outcome than an unthrottled OTP endpoint; (4) proof-of-work — taxes the slowest legitimate device hardest. **The enumeration analysis is written down** rather than left to be re-derived: during saturation an unseen identifier is refused while a tracked one is served, which distinguishes 'requested a code recently', NOT 'this account exists' — the OTP path never consults the registry (`subject_for` is created on first successful VERIFY), so real and invented identifiers are treated identically by construction, and a real user who has not signed in this hour is untracked exactly like a fabricated address. No new oracle. Key DELIVERY reuses `/v1/envelopes/{subject_id}` (chosen over minting a parallel mechanism): the wrapped key is one envelope row per recipient, upsert-by-recipient, wholesale replace for removal — the existing rotation route is what revocation wiring inherits. **THE ENVELOPE PAYLOAD IS CLIENT-LAYER (§6.4):** `{"v":1,"from":<sender device id>,"wrapped":<hex>}` — the unwrap needs the SENDER's public key and carries it here, keeping the relay untrusted and unaware. The DEVICE id is the vault's existing 16-byte `sync/device-id` (the HLC author identity — one identity per device across the whole engine). **BOTH SHELLS AS TWINS (`DeviceKeyService`):** bootstrap at sign-in = ensure keypair (core-born, persisted; the secret NEVER leaves the device) → publish → receive-or-found. The identifier `google:{sub}` goes through the same session tail as Apple's (`mint_verified_session`, extracted from `auth_apple` unchanged). Unconfigured is closed: with no `SKIPTI_GOOGLE_*_CLIENT_ID`, start refuses and nothing verifies, and each path stays closed until its own client id is set. New inside `LedgerStore.kt` (its internals are private): `MemberDTO`, `SelfDTO`, `GroupDTO.memberNames` (optional; `explicitNulls = false` keeps old vaults decoding), `ledger/self`, `ledger/selected-group`, and the same surface as iOS (`loadSelf`/`ensureSelf` with legacy-Ada adoption, `setYourName`, `namedGroups` with per-member names and "Member N" placeholders, `createGroup`, `addMember`, `renameMember`, `selectGroup`, `currentGroup`, `label` → "Tim (You)"). `loadGroups()` now THROWS `LedgerCorruptException` on an unreadable list; it used to return `emptyList()`. `GroupScreens.kt`: YourNameScreen, CreateGroupScreen, GroupListScreen (with People inside), PeopleScreen and `GroupCopy`, all with copy identical to iOS, as routes over HomeShell's tabs. Screens: Balance has the NEEDS_NAME / NO_GROUPS / READY states and a group chip; Add has a PAID BY chip row, everyone on and the group's currency; Settle and Expenses use the group's names and your id. `buildExpense` takes `payer` and `groupId` and reads no vault; `buildSpec`'s Payer only uses the chosen payer; `SettleUi.recomputePlan` takes the viewer; `SettleUi.settlementFor` builds the settlement from your id. **Findings:** (1) **A failed settlement was silently dropped**: `recordSettlement` caught every exception with "surfaced by the load-error path on the next recompute", but no recompute ever ran, so the button stayed "Settling…" for good. Failures now show an owed-colour line and reset the button, and nothing can escape the coroutine (the FireAndForgetGuard lesson). (3) The data-loss pattern in `loadGroupsOrSeed` (corrupt list overwritten with the fixture group) is now reachable only from proof surfaces, and is marked as such. | D-137 | **Gate speed: the pre-commit hook stops repeating proven work, the quick checks run on every commit, and every gate leg is timed.** The founder asked why checks took 30+ minutes. Measured: macOS `syspolicyd` assesses every proc-macro dylib and new test binary (clippy 16m37s for one crate; a 12m44s test run for ~10 s of tests), which only the founder's Developer Tools setting can remove; and every unit commit re-ran clippy, cargo test and wasm on Rust a full gate had just passed. New `scripts/gate_inputs.py` fingerprints the heavy inputs (every file git sees except a DENYLIST of paths cargo never reads, so anything new counts) plus the toolchain. `gate.sh` writes `.git/skipti-heavy-legs-pass.json` only after a fast or full run with nothing failed or skipped whose inputs did not change during the run, and deletes it otherwise; it gains `--cheap`, `(Ns)` per leg and a Timing table after the evidence. The hook runs the six cheap legs on every commit, and the heavy legs when a staged change (deletions included) touches a heavy input, unless the INDEX's fingerprint equals the proof. **Findings:** (1) **the Developer Tools exemption was not reaching the gate** (R1 fast gate 20m37s; 191 `GK evaluateScanResult` in 10 min; Apple connections 45–86 s), reported to the founder; (2) the scan costs first loads: cached clippy took 0 s and already-seen test binaries ran in seconds; (3) the self-test must scrub git's environment, because inside the hook `GIT_INDEX_FILE` would point its `git add` at the real index; (4) the old hook ran nothing for a check-script-, BUILD-LOG- or Swift-only commit, missed staged deletions, and skipped `include_str!` inputs; (5) three runbook mistakes from the 2026-09-18 relay upgrade (the backup glob run unprivileged, `git rev-parse` on a box with no checkout, "uncomment" lines that did not exist), fixed with a new "Updating a running relay" §7.1; (6) D-135's five "D-137" pointers corrected in place to "expected D-139". Real runs: R1 pass wrote the proof and `check-index` matched the staged scripts; R2 (stub cargo, rustfmt fails) cleared it; R3 (edit during the run) wrote nothing. New gate leg `scripts/test_gate_inputs.py` (21 tests, ~4 s, including the real hook against a stub gate): **18 legs**. **Sabotage 10/10** on the first run. | Unit commits no longer wait on proven work; the gate reports where its time goes; the gaps that let a commit skip every check are closed | `scripts/gate_inputs.py`, `scripts/test_gate_inputs.py`, `scripts/gate.sh`, `.githooks/pre-commit`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/DEPLOY-ORACLE.md`, `docs/BUILD-LOG.md` (D-135 corrections), `docs/WORKLOG.md` |

| D-178 | **Your phones share one account: a phone signed in to your account gets your data by itself, Maximum security makes it ask first, and SKIPTI syncs every 10 seconds and on pull.** The founder signed in with Google on his iPhone (a group, a $100 expense) and on his Android phone with the same account: the Android phone showed nothing. **Two root causes, both since D-123:** (1) Apple, Google and email sign-ins send `sync_device_id: null` (deliberately, so D-168's other-account check runs first), so the relay session had no device and `PUT /v1/devices/agreement-key` answered 401; each phone then synced under a random key of its own and no phone could ever be given the account's key. Shells (twins): the transports send the body for every method but GET; sync attaches the device first; `refresh()` heals a phone without the account key, pulls, pushes and shares, and reports a `SyncReport`; a pull skips entries it cannot open once the phone holds the account key (a never-authorised phone still fails closed); a phone that receives a different key resets its push cursor so its own records go up again. **The founder's decisions (2026-09-29):** automatic by default (a phone holding the key wraps it to every new phone of the account on its next sync) with a notice on the old phone ("Your data was shared with a new phone", six words, "Not you? | D-218 | **The two D-210 leftovers: zero-net loops leave the People cards, and the cloud refuses an invite for a place a member already holds (plan `2026-10-16-d218-d210-leftovers.md`; built in the session 4 run while the founder was away, so the decisions taken for him are listed below).** The founder's ask (2026-10-16): "hide zero-net loops on People cards (core removes equal cycles from the pairwise view; totals unchanged); refuse invites for a place a member already holds (the app never offers it; createInvite, inviteUser and inviteKnown refuse with a clear message; a refusal test in firebase/tests, a CLOUD-SECURITY row the same day; it deploys with 0.5.0, not before)". (1) **Core.** `norn::cancel_cycles` beside `collapse`: a depth-first search for a directed cycle (start nodes and each node's creditors in ascending participant id; the first edge back into the path closes it), the cycle's smallest edge subtracted from every edge on it, zeros dropped, a fresh search, until no cycle is left; a `debug_assert!` on positive entries. Called once per currency matrix in `ffi::balance_line`, after D-210's removed-person collapse, so every pairwise view (Home's People cards through `overview`, the group page, Settle up, Removal's settle-first, GroupSettings) takes it and no shell computes anything. Nets, `viewer_net_minor`, `transfers` and totals are untouched by construction; no entry is added and none grows. No FFI signature change and no core version bump; the bindings were regenerated only because UniFFI copies the `BalanceLineOut` doc comment into them (8d58bfa, comments only, found by the first full gate). SPEC 5.6 gains a paragraph. 12 new core tests: goldens G1 to G6, L1 and L2, re-derived independently in `.drafts/d218/cycles.py` from the plan's algorithm text (it also re-implements D-210's collapse from its doc comment; 2,000 seeded matrices, 877 with a loop, hold every postcondition), and a 500-matrix seeded property test (same nets, no new key, no larger amount, no cycle by an independent sink-removal search, idempotent). Records are never rewritten; a phone with no account behaves exactly as before (the D-152 and D-153 goldens unedited).** (1) **The bug** (the plan's reading of the tree, verified): since D-153 a phone adopts the account's earliest "you" (y) across phones, but a group made under this phone's own id (x) has x as its member; the phone kept writing y as payer, shares, `addedBy`, settlement ends, renames and redistributions, which the other members' phones store and show as "Unknown member", with y carried as an extra person, x's debt unmoved and a settlement from y not applied (core does not refuse it: `norn::Ledger::apply_expense`'s `NonMemberPayer` is the tests' oracle only). L1b: `ownClaims` claimed the MERGED "you", not a raw member there, so core filed it as pending and every push wrote another one. Two cases for records already written: (i) no claim on x yet, so the fixed `ownClaims` writes `{x, you y}`, the first claim on x, and D-158's claim alias makes every y record readable on every build, 0.4.0 included; (ii) `{x, you x}` already stands (the phone with the older "you" signed in second), a second claim is contested and core cannot tell it is the same account: only the server can (Phase B). (2) **The design**: core computes, per group, the account's `place` (the raw member that is its own there: "you" if raw, present and not claimed by another; else the first winning claim naming one of its ids on a present member; else the first raw member among its ids) and `you_as` (the place whenever "you" is not readable there); each shell maps only what goes into the RECORD (payer, shares collapsed by core, `addedBy`, editor, settlement ends, redistribution `from` and shares, `renameMember`, `removeMember`), never the kv ledger, through one `Placing` value that is a REQUIRED parameter of every record builder and of `appendGroupOps`, so the compiler finds every writer (the backfills and personal writers pass `Placing.none` / `NONE` written out); `ownClaims` claims the place; Phase B (A1, the founder's fork F1, option A taken for him): a new group op `placeAlias` `{"op":"placeAlias","group":G,"member":x,"you":y}` that phones build but never upload, written only by a new callable `shareAliases` with the server's mark `alias: true` (which `validRecord`'s `hasOnly` already refuses from a phone; no rules change), after the server checks x is the caller's place (D-227's `holderIn`, decisions 36 and 37, A2), y is the caller's own id and nobody else's; phones import it only with the mark and ask only for ids a record of that group already uses (`AliasShare`, once per group and id, `alias.share.answered`). | D-230 | **Held places: the server's word on who holds a place, so a phone-written claim can no longer take or deny anyone's place or history in a group (CLOUD-SECURITY G-08, the D-229 residue; the founder's call in session 7: the G-08 unit is built BEFORE 0.5.0, approach "A plus the join-time mark"; spec `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-18-d230-held-places.md` and plan `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-18-d230-held-places.md`, ec97578 and b7296e3; controller amendments A1 to A10 in `.superpowers/sdd/d230/amendments.md`; built 2026-10-18 in the session 7 run, finished 2026-10-19 in session 8). Nothing deployed: the Functions, the rules (unchanged) and the apps reach production at 0.5.0.** (1) **The problem**: who a member IS (which account, which "you" id) was decided by phone-written `claim` records ordered by a record identity the phone chooses, so a claim written before the victim's own (backdated, or honestly early by someone who already knew the id) made the victim's group read-only (decision 44) and, once the forger's member left, read the victim's history as the forger's on every phone; core cannot tell such a claim from an honest one, only the server knows whose an id is. (2) **The design** (D-229's marked alias applied to the place): a new group op `heldPlace` `{"op":"heldPlace","group":G,"member":m,"you":y}` ("place m is held by the account whose id is y") that phones build and never upload, written only by the server with the mark `held: true` (`validRecord`'s `hasOnly` already refuses it from a phone; a refusal test pins it; no rules change) after checking the caller holds the place and owns the id, its record identity stamped by the server; core treats a marked held place as final for its member and its id: every unmarked claim on that member with another id, or naming that id on another member, is void (reported `contested`), and decisions 44 to 51 run over what is left. Two writers: a new callable **`sharePlaces`** (the phones' `PlaceShare` job, `AliasShare`'s twin, after a push) and **`acceptInvite`**, which takes the join's built records and writes them marked in the join's own transaction. Now per group: `claimed_in`, the member merge and `placing` per group, the claimed places emitted as aliases (group, place, you) that the FFI merges apply per group (`Yous::with_aliases` drops such an id from the global set), `other_you_ids` unchanged for the shells; both shells' `Placing.mineIn(group)` leaves out the places claimed only elsewhere. A2 (Medium, core, decision 132): after a received stamp at T a phone's next ids were (T, c+1), (T, c+2) ... with its device id in every record, so a co-member could list the next thousand in a revision's `seen` and pre-empt every edit of that phone to that expense for a day (D-235 had rated the attack as needing an exact millisecond); `Hlc::tick_by` adds a 20-bit random step per own stamp (`ffi_hlc_next` draws it; the carry at the low 24 bits, never into the era), a next id one guess in about a million; no wire or FFI change (a doc comment on the export would have changed its UniFFI checksum: made a plain comment, the bindings byte-identical). Fixed by pinning the negative to entropy [0x42; 16] (the same fix mnemonic.rs got in D-49); the generate path is tested POSITIVELY only. | At rest, the vault leaks nothing — and the key exists nowhere on disk | `cargo test -p skipti-core skrin::tests::at_rest` + `keystore_destroy` | A-17 headless half (D-39): canary plaintext and amount absent from vault bytes; raw and hex database key absent from vault bytes; the key lives only behind the Keystore trait (no export path exists); destroy zeroizes. Device backup-exclusion enforcement and biometric unlock are Phase 7 shell work — see §4.2 |
| Account deletion removes every trace — proven by querying the store across a restart | `cargo test -p skipti-server --test delete_account_http` + direct SQL against the temp vault | D-62/§4.4: ada (real SoftPasskey ceremony) and grace (OTP) share a group; ada also owns a solo group. Deletion via one authenticated call: her bearer and refresh die immediately; grace loses NOTHING (logs byte-identical, escrow intact, her envelope rows remain, ada's gone, the solo group destroyed); direct SQLite counts go [1,1,2,1,1,2,1] → [0;7]; after a full close/reopen the identical queries still answer [0;7] while grace reads exactly her pre-deletion data; re-signing-in as ada mints a NEW subject with an empty bucket. Row-level proof only — see D-62 for the honest WAL note |
| Sign in with Apple: verified identity tokens mint sessions bound to Apple's sub | `cargo test -p skipti-server --test apple_http` (+ `ios/SkiptiTests/RelayClientTests`) | D-63/§12.2: genuine RS256 tokens from a pinned test keypair against a local JWKS server — happy path attributes through the registry and refreshes; seven failure modes reject with ONE body; unknown-kid forces refetch (impostor key published mid-test); deleted accounts restart fresh (D-62 interlock); parse failures never touch the network. iOS: snake_case request pinned as decoded shape (§5.13), uniform rejection, E2E vs live relay rejects fabricated tokens; the on-device ASAuthorization ceremony waits on entitlement+AASA+TLS (§4.4), covered server-side here |

### D-120 audited cold — the last shell divergence closed — 2026-08-29

Gate re-run independently at `00c8005`: **14/14, 0 skipped**.

**Verified, not accepted:** `identifier` is genuinely **deleted** from
`PasskeyFinishBody` (only `challenge_id` + `response` remain) rather than
ignored; `startRegistration` no longer takes an identifier at all and carries
the bearer; `finishRegistration` carries it too (two `bearer: accessToken`
sites, no more); both sign-in legs remain bearerless. Sabotage confirms the
guard bites — nulling the first bearer fails `make ios-app` at the
start-contract test.

**The honest finding corrects the paste that asked for the work.** The paste
said "the transport needs a way to carry a bearer if it has none". It already
had one: `RelayHTTPRequest.bearer` has existed since D-55 and is how
`SyncService` and `IdentityService` already authenticate. So D-102's omission
was never blocked by anything — the field was sitting there. That makes the
original miss slightly worse and the fix much smaller than budgeted, and it
is worth recording in that direction rather than the flattering one.

**§5.23's recorded cost is recovered.** That incident noted the served
`rp.id` was no longer assertable live, because reading it now needs a session
and production never exposes an OTP code. D-120 recovers it the only
legitimate way: against a **dev-flagged local relay**, mint a real session
through `/v1/dev/session`, drive `register/start` with its bearer, and assert
the served RP ID. Production's bearerless-refusal assertion is left exactly
as written. A cost that gets recorded and then quietly stays paid is a
different thing from one that gets recovered; this is the second.

**Their own method note is the right one:** a first sabotage round was
refused by Swift's memberwise init at COMPILE time — the wrong red — and was
redone so the assertion itself refused. That is the same trap §3 records
twice against the audit, caught independently here.

**Both shells now hold D-102's contract identically.** The divergence that
produced §5.23 is closed on the side that had it wrong.

### D-119 audited cold — 2026-08-29

Gate re-run independently at `c97c645`: **14/14, 0 skipped**. JVM
**206 executions = 103 tests x 2 variants**, 0 failed.

**GUARANTEES #4 is now true on both shells.** Export was the right thing to
do first: it closes a PUBLISHED guarantee ("exportable in full, in an open
format, at any time, in one tap"), where import is a feature. An Android build
without export made a published claim false for that shell.

**§9.4's gate is structural and it bites.** Removing
`if (!acknowledged) throw NotAcknowledged()` reddens exactly
`an_unacknowledged_export_writes_nothing`. The shape is right: the refusal
lives in `export()` with no parameter, default or flag that lowers it, and
the screen's obligation (rendering the flat-loss line) is deliberately
separate from the gate that must never lower. Deriving `flatLosses` from the
snapshot rather than a hand-maintained flag is the same discipline.

**Timezone question answered while auditing** (the box runs UTC): nothing
depends on a local zone. `SystemTime::now()` is epoch-based and zone-free,
`skipti-backup.sh` already stamps with `date -u`, no `Local::now` or
`localtime` appears in `core/` or `server/`, and no test reads `TZ`. UTC on a
server is also the correct choice, not merely a tolerable one — D-119's own
export filenames pin a UTC date across a local-midnight boundary for exactly
this reason.

**AUDIT METHOD NOTE, again the same family.** The first sabotage of the §9.4
gate used a regex that did not match; the file was untouched and the run
reported `0 RED`. That is a NON-RESULT, not a pass, and it was caught only
because the probe printed whether its anchor matched. The lesson is now
mechanical rather than aspirational: **a sabotage must assert its own edit
landed before the result means anything** — the same rule §3 already carries
for reading regenerated artifacts, applied one step earlier in the chain.

### Android's passkey prerequisite is LIVE — 2026-08-29

`assetlinks.json` is served from the RP ID and **accepted by Google's own
Digital Asset Links validator**: two statements, both
`delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds`, zero errors. Verified through
the API rather than by reading the file, because a file that parses and a
file Google accepts are different claims:

```
statements accepted: 2
  com.vardrlabs.skipti          delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds
  com.vardrlabs.skipti.direct   delegate_permission/common.get_login_creds
errors/warnings: 0
```

Both application ids are authorised — ADR-0010 makes `direct` a real
distribution channel, and both flavours share the upload key. Procedure
recorded as `DEPLOY-ORACLE.md` §8.1, deliberately WITHOUT the fingerprint
value: it is public, but embedding it would make the runbook silently wrong
the day the key is replaced, exactly as `<PUBLIC_IP>` is a placeholder
everywhere else.

**Where this leaves the two ceremonies.** Both shells now have their
host-side prerequisite met — iOS's AASA has been live since D-81, Android's
asset links as of today. What remains is device-side and identical in shape
on both: a real handset with a screen lock and a credential provider. The
`CreateCredentialNoCreateOptionException` D-118 saw on the emulator is
correct behaviour for a device without one, not a defect.

The upload keystore that produced the fingerprint also signs the Play upload,
so one founder-side action unblocked both the Android ceremony and Play
packaging. It lives outside the repo and is not in any agent's hands.

### D-118 audited cold — 2026-08-28

Gate re-run independently at `fdb4bdb`: **14/14, 0 skipped**.

**D-102's contract is right from the first line on Android, which iOS still
is not.** `register/start` carries the bearer and sends NO body; the JVM
negative asserts the string `identifier` appears nowhere in the finish body.
Sabotage confirms the guard bites: replacing the bearer with `null` reddens
exactly `enrolment_start_carries_the_bearer_and_no_identifier`. The second
shell got the contract correct on its first attempt because the first shell's
mistake had been written down — which is the whole argument for recording
incidents rather than just fixing them.

**The allowlist fired on a real third-party library, for the first time.**
`androidx.credentials` declares `USE_BIOMETRIC` and `USE_FINGERPRINT` in its
own manifest (the Credential Manager consent step), and D-116's check failed
exactly as designed. This is the vindication of choosing an ALLOWLIST over
the SMS blocklist the paste specified: a blocklist would have accepted both
silently, and would accept whatever the next library brings. Extended
deliberately, in the open, both normal-level; SMS sweep verified untouched.

**The dependency was taken correctly** (rule 4): `androidx.credentials:1.5.0`
is the platform's documented passkey API, replaces nothing, and the
alternatives named — GMS's deprecated `Fido2ApiClient`, or a hand-rolled
WebAuthn client — are both worse. Deferring `credentials-play-services-auth`
until the device work is the right call: an unused provider artifact is an
untested one.

**The honest limit is stated on both shells and neither pretends.** The
completing ceremony needs a real device, a screen lock, a credential provider
and digital-asset-links hosting for the RP ID. `CreateCredentialNoCreateOptionException`
in logcat is exactly what an emulator without a provider should produce, and
reading it as proof of the bearer'd leg succeeding — rather than as a failure
to hide — is the right use of it.

### D-117 audited cold — 2026-08-28

Gate re-run independently at `69aeb87`, **after the deploy**: **14/14, 0
skipped**, `make ios-app TEST SUCCEEDED`. The leg that was red for a true
reason cleared itself when production became correct.

**D-117's headline finding was right, and bigger than it looked.** It reported
the iOS leg failing against a reachable relay via D-102's 401. The mechanism
was exactly right and the relay was production, not `:8080` — which is how
incident §5.23 was found: the fix had never been deployed. Reporting a leg
failure it could not fully diagnose, instead of dodging it, is what surfaced a
live vulnerability.

**D-27 is pinned structurally, and the pin bites.** `IdentityTest` asserts by
reflection that `RelayError.Rejected` declares **zero instance fields**, that
the sealed family is exactly the five expected shapes, and — the subtle one —
that `ServerError` is the only stateful member and carries only `status`,
since a 5xx says nothing about any account's existence. Sabotage confirms:
giving `Rejected` a `why` field reddens exactly
`the_rejection_type_cannot_say_why`. A type that cannot express the difference
is a stronger guarantee than copy that declines to mention it.

**The INTERNET allowlist extension was the right call, taken in the open.**
D-116's script demanded that any later permission "narrow this allowlist
DELIBERATELY, in the open", and that is what happened. INTERNET is
normal-level and install-time — no prompt, outside the runtime permission
model, not sensitive in ADR-0016's sense (that rule confines SENSITIVE
permissions to updates). The app cannot open a socket without it, so the
declaration is the honest statement of what D-117 made the app do. The SMS
sweep is untouched and the allowlist is still an allowlist: verified that
`ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` still fails the check.

**Three defects only the emulator caught** — `ProcessHandle` absent on
Android, the missing INTERNET permission, and a missing `remember()` racing
the proof screen. All three are invisible to JVM tests by construction, which
is the same boundary D-112's saver crash sat on: `make android-test` proves
Kotlin logic against real core and does not execute the platform.

### D-116 audited cold — 2026-08-28

Gate re-run independently at `8271aa1`: **14/14, 0 skipped**. Swift 96.

**The allowlist is better than what the paste asked for, and it is
demonstrated.** The paste specified "no SMS permission in the merged
manifest". D-116 built an ALLOWLIST of exactly one entry instead, reasoning
that an SMS blocklist would pass a manifest carrying any other surprise
permission from a future library. Verified by sabotage: adding
`ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION` — not SMS-shaped at all — to the play source manifest
makes the merged manifest carry it and the check exit 1. **A blocklist would
have passed that.** The first run's failure on the toolchain's own
auto-generated permission is the same point arriving unbidden.

**Signing hygiene holds:** nothing tracked, `keystore.properties` gitignored,
credentials read from env or that file, and no credentials means an UNSIGNED
AAB — the correct stop state, as instructed.

**Version scheme checked arithmetically:** `major x 1e6 + minor x 1e3 + patch`
gives 0.1.0 -> 1000 and 1.0.0 -> 1,000,000, which exceeds every 0.x code
(max 999,999). Monotonic as claimed, and 1.0.0 really does clear the 0.x range.

**AUDIT CORRECTION TO THE TALLY — the audit's own defect, D-108's family
again.** "136 JVM tests" is **68 tests run against 2 flavour variants**, not

### D-114 audited cold — 2026-08-28

Gate re-run independently at `52f2b88`: **14/14, 0 skipped**. JVM 65/0
(SyncTest 10 joining); Swift 96.

**The two claims that had to be true are true.**

*No new dependency* — `android/app/build.gradle.kts` was not touched at all by
the commit, so `cargo deny` and the SBOM leg are untouched and the
`HttpURLConnection` decision cost nothing. The reasoning in the D-114 row is
sound: the transport boundary confines the client to one class, so the
smallest supply chain that does the job honestly is the right one.

*Only ciphertext reaches the relay* — traced the push path end to end:
`currentEnvelope()` → `reserveSealCounter()` → `ffiSyncSeal(...)` → and the
request body carries `HexCodec.encode(sealed)` and nothing else. No raw kv
value is ever sent. GUARANTEES #7 holds by construction here.

**The nonce ordering is right, and it is the security-critical detail of the
unit.** `reserveSealCounter` persists `next` and only then returns it, so a
crash between reservation and use WASTES a counter and never reuses one. In
AES-GCM a reused (key, nonce) is catastrophic, so the crash-safe direction is
the only acceptable one. Sabotage confirms the guard bites: dropping the
`rawKvSet` before the return reddens
`seal_counter_persists_before_use_waste_never_reuse`.

**All three reported sabotages reproduce exactly, each on the right test:**

| sabotage | red |
|---|---|
| counter used before it is persisted | 1 — `seal_counter_persists_before_use_waste_never_reuse` |
| pull 401 returns an empty list | 1 — `a_pull_failure_throws_rather_than_masquerading_as_an_empty_bucket` |
| push 409 treated as a failure | 1 — `a_409_is_normal_conflict_not_a_failure` |

The 401 one deserves its name: a restore that read "unauthorized" as "nothing
there" would wipe the state it was restoring. That is the sharpest hazard in
the unit and it is guarded.

**The offline requirement is properly proven**, which was the thing this
audit pushed hardest for. `offline_leaves_the_ledger_fully_usable` drives a
transport that fails, asserts `State.Offline`, asserts `pushLatest` returns
false rather than throwing, and then asserts the ledger still reads and still
accepts a write. Emulator evidence matches.

**NEW FINDING — the fire-and-forget path's crash-safety is unguarded.**
`LedgerSync.fireAndForget` runs on BOTH save paths (`AddExpenseScreen.kt:465`,
`SettleScreen.kt:314`) inside `CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch`, and its
`try/catch` around `pushLatest` is what stops a background failure reaching the
default handler — where, on Android, an uncaught exception in a launched
coroutine crashes the process.

Replacing that `catch` with `finally { }` — so the exception propagates —
leaves the suite **0 RED across all 65 tests**. No test calls `fireAndForget`
at all; the only mention in `SyncTest.kt` is a comment. So the catch is
correct, load-bearing, and unprotected: a future edit that "tidies" it away
ships green.

Same class as D-112's saver blind spot: a real runtime failure mode, on the
actual user path, invisible to the JVM suite. Handed to the product lane with
the fix named rather than written here — a test that invokes `fireAndForget`
with a throwing transport and asserts it returns without propagating.

**AUDIT PROBE ERRORS, recorded because two of four were wrong.** Mutating the
restore path's `state = State.Offline` proved nothing — that catch already
rethrows, so the mutation was near-vacuous. Mutating `else -> Outcome.Offline`
proved nothing either: that branch handles an unexpected HTTP STATUS, while
the offline test exercises a transport that never returns a response at all.
Both were reported as "0 RED" internally before being understood, and neither
is evidence of a gap. The rule from §3 stands and needed applying twice more:
know which path a mutation is on before reading its result.

### D-113 audited cold — the blind spot is CLOSED, measured — 2026-08-27

Gate re-run independently at `499722d`: **14/14, 0 skipped**. JVM 55/0
(SaverRoundTripTest 2 joining); Swift 96.

**The verdict on §3's proven blind spot, measured the same way it was
opened.** The audit's exact D-112 mutation — `@Serializable` stripped from
`Exact`, which produced **0 RED across all 53 tests** while the app crashed on
launch — now produces:

```
-> 1 RED
   every_sealed_subclass_round_trips_through_the_savers_json
```

Closed. Same mutation, same command, opposite result.

**The sweep is genuinely reflective**, not a hand-listed set wearing
reflection's clothes: `SplitDraft::class.sealedSubclasses` iterated in a
`for` loop. `kotlin-reflect` is `testImplementation` — verified test-scope
only, so nothing new ships in the APK.

**"Checked, none" holds.** Every other `rememberSaveable` in the shell
(Onboarding's five, the tab index, the add form's primitives) stores a
platform type — `String`, `String?`, `Boolean`, `List<String>`, `List<Int>`,
`Map<Int, String>`. `SplitDraft` was the only custom-class saver, so it was
the only one exposed to this failure.

**A stronger guard than expected, found while probing the future case.** A new
`SplitDraft` subclass cannot be added silently at all: it fails to COMPILE at
**three** separate exhaustive `when` sites, each demanding a branch. The
compiler stops a half-wired subclass before any test runs — a better guard
than the test, because it cannot be skipped.

**Stated as unproven rather than implied:** the audit did NOT manage to
verify the remaining case — a FULLY wired new subclass whose `@Serializable`
is forgotten. Five successive probes died on type errors in the wiring the
audit was fabricating (`SplitSpecInput` inference, `when` exhaustiveness), and
the probe was abandoned rather than reported as a result. The mechanism makes
it very likely — an unannotated subclass is in `sealedSubclasses`, and
`Json.encodeToString` throws on it exactly as it did for `Exact` — but "very
likely" is not "measured", and this log distinguishes them. Anyone wiring an
eighth subclass should watch this test fail once, deliberately.

That the fabricated probes kept failing is itself the finding above: the type
system makes a half-wired subclass genuinely hard to write.

demonstrated, not argued.** D-112's first emulator launch CRASHED: the

Full gate re-run independently at `c1a03ff`: **14/14, 0 skipped**. JVM 25/0
(BalanceScreenTest 8, KitCodecTest 6, LedgerStoreTest 11); Swift **96 tests,
8 skipped, 0 failures** — the eight are SyncE2ETests' honest relay-down skip.
The cross-shell golden test appears in the Swift run, so the file really is

**Sabotage matrix re-run at the boundary, and the result is mixed in an
instructive way:**

| claim | reproduced? |
|---|---|

On the third: four attempts to make the codec "strict" all left the suite
GREEN — `ignoreUnknownKeys = false`, `explicitNulls = true`, stripping the
property defaults, and both together. The reason is the finding:
**kotlinx.serialization and Swift's `JSONDecoder` are both inherently
tolerant of an absent key for an OPTIONAL property**, and that shared
behaviour is precisely the cross-shell property the golden pins. No
configuration knob turns it off.

Two controls settle that the guard is nevertheless real, so this is not a
check that cannot fail: breaking `decodeEnvelope` outright reddens **5** —
matching the reported count exactly, and identifying it as a decode-path
mutation — and the REALISTIC regression, making `note` non-nullable, reddens
**3** including both goldens. The guard bites on the mutation that will
actually happen one day (a field made required); it does not bite on
configuration, because configuration cannot break it.

Recorded rather than left implicit, and written INTO both tests, because the
audit burned four runs discovering it and the next reader should not: probe
this guard by making a field required, not by flipping decoder settings.

**Also caught here, and it was the audit's own defect:** D-108's gate leg
passed a STATIC `"14 passed, 0 failed"` as its evidence-block detail. D-109
took the count to 25, so the evidence block — the exact text this project
pastes into §3 as proof — would have printed a false tally. D-109 fixed it to
point at the leg's own printout. That is the fourth check-that-lies caught in
this stretch, and the second one authored by the audit rather than found by it.

The offline proof, hardest as ordered:
- JVM: with a transport that THROWS (connection refused), `pushLatest`
  returns false into `.Offline`, nothing escapes — and the ledger stays
  fully usable: an expense saves through the real vault loop, the balance
  computes (1,250 USD owed), the note reads back.
- On the emulator with NO relay reachable: fresh install → onboarding →
  §11.6 empty home → add 8.40 USD → save (the hook fires, lands offline
  silently) → the home balance renders $4.20 owed — `offline-usable.png`.
  Logcat clean.

Stub-transport suite (SyncTest, 10): unauthenticated push is ONE
rejection with the request shape asserted (subject-1 bucket, raw token,
hex body — D-41 + §6.4); 409 is Conflict at the entry's index (D-18);
pull-401 THROWS (never an empty bucket); malformed body THROWS; no
session → the hook is a no-op and stays Idle; envelope seal/open byte
identity through core; a restore writes the raw kv bytes VERBATIM; the
seal counter persists BEFORE use (waste, never reuse — asserted across
two attempts); u64BE round trip; RelayConfig resolve goldens (production
default, --relay-local, https-only override honoured, malformed/
cleartext overrides fall to production rather than degrading).

Sabotage matrix, build success verified before reading results:
- pull reading 401 as an empty bucket → exactly
  `a_pull_failure_throws_rather_than_masquerading_as_an_empty_bucket`.
- 409 mapped to Outcome.Offline → exactly
  `a_409_is_normal_conflict_not_a_failure`.
- the seal counter REUSED instead of reserved → exactly
  `seal_counter_persists_before_use_waste_never_reuse`.

WHAT CANNOT BE PROVEN, stated plainly: a full authenticated push→pull
round trip needs a session, and the relay never exposes the OTP code —
it goes out of band. iOS records exactly this limit; no test here claims
more. The dev-mint round trip lands with the sign-in screens that can
mint a session.

THE FINDINGS THE PROOFS FORCED, recorded because they are the design:

- **The HLC receive rule sets the honest boundary of "offline."** The
  first offline-position test created the "offline" record AFTER the
  device had merged a 9_000 stamp — and the record correctly stamped
  (9_000, c+1), sorting after what the device had SEEN. That is the HLC
  working as designed (a total order needs it); the pure offline
  scenario — create before ANY contact — is what the test now proves,
  and the boundary is stated in the test's comment.
- **Group ids are per-device today**, so the three-device proof compares
  per-currency ledger totals (identical) rather than group-scoped
  balance containers. Group RECORDS are the follow-up unit (§4).

  ASCII plaintext, and ASCII plaintext never appears inside its own hex
  encoding. The sabotage (push unsealed) sailed through green. Hardened
  to decode the stored bytes the relay would hold — then the sabotage
  went red. The same discipline as "a check that can fail" (§4's rule),
  applied to a test that looked right and was not.

THE FIXES, one paragraph each — the full decision record is the D-122
row in §2:

- **#0, the stubs:** both MemoryRelay stubs became the real relay's
  contract — a map keyed by index, per-entry accept-and-count (a batch
  carrying the same index twice is refused, not excused), 409 exactly
  when accepted < entries.size, and the real response body
  `{"accepted":N,"next_index":M}`. The old list shape is what excused #1.
- **#1, the index:** base taken once per batch, each record stamps
  base+i (both shells); the push outcome prefers the server's
  authoritative next_index (the client's max+1 is the fallback);
  the 409 reconcile reuses pullAndMerge's pull (MergeResult carries
  maxPulledIndex) instead of issuing a second full pull.
- **#2, the HLC offset:** `LedgerStore.Sync.decodeHlcState` is the ONLY
  decoder for the persisted `u64BE(millis) ‖ u32BE(counter)` state —
  all three iOS call sites (pushedHlcCursor, nextHlc, receiveHlc) go
  through it, and `u32FromBE` preconditions on exactly 4 bytes so the
  offset cannot drift apart again.
- **#3, the backfill:** `backfillLegacyRecords` (both shells) runs at
  the top of every pull, BEFORE anything is applied: legacy kv rows are
  minted into records unless the record path already holds the same row
  (decoded-blob equality — idempotent), each stamped from its OWN
  expense timestamp with this device as author, so it keeps its
  position and is pushable.

THE PROOFS ADDED (twins on both shells unless noted): the multi-record
push (A pushes three; B, never pulled, pushes three through a 409
reconcile; the relay holds SIX entries at SIX distinct indices; a fresh
device restores all six in HLC order; a settled cursor pushes nothing);
three same-millisecond records keep distinct identities, pinned at
PRODUCTION magnitude 1_788_134_400_000 (the comment in the test states
why: below 2^32 the old misread returned 0 and the collision only bites
from the third same-millisecond record on — two records could never
fail); the iOS HLC codec golden (round-trip at production magnitude,
naming the misread it forbids: the top four bytes decode to 416); and
the upgrade test (a kv-only vault pulls, its legacy expense and
settlement survive AND become pushable records; the wire carries one
bounded at-least-once duplicate and a fresh device converges on exactly
three distinct records).

THE PROOF THAT REMOVED THE CRUTCH: at least one record-sync proof per
shell no longer shares a fixture secret — two devices, each generating
its OWN agreement keypair, converge on the same ledger BECAUSE THE
ENVELOPE PATH CARRIED THE KEY. The founder mints and self-wraps; the
newcomer is gated (it holds no account key and the relay records no
log-push request from it — the tight anchor); the founder authorises
through the envelope surface; the newcomer receives on its next sign-in
with its OWN seal session; both converge. GUARANTEES #7 through the new
path: the relay's stored envelope bytes contain neither ledger plaintext
nor a 32-byte window of the raw key. The negative bites: a
never-authorised device's restore THROWS fail-closed (the open refusing,
never an empty read), its local ledger survives, and the same device
recovers completely once authorised.

| iOS: the push gate removed — FIRST ATTEMPT | **the test PASSED — the deviation**. The 409-then-open-refusal path masks the missing gate (the unauthorised push fails anyway, for the wrong reason). The proof gained the tight anchor (the relay recorded no log-push request from the unauthorised device) and the SAME sabotage then went red. Recorded because a guard whose absence is masked by accident is guarded twice or not at all |
| iOS: the push gate removed, with the tight anchor | exactly the two-device test red |

THE THREE D-122-AUDIT CLEANUPS, taken here: (1) iOS
`LedgerSync.u32FromBE` — dead code still reading `prefix(4)`, the exact
shape of the D-122 bug — deleted; (2) the 3-char canaries (`INR`,
`payer`) in the ciphertext test replaced with distinctive long tokens on
both shells — the 32-char payer id is a VALUE in any plaintext DTO
serialization regardless of JSON key order; the 3-char fragments were
probabilistic (p ≈ N x 2^-24), which is the audit's own correction to
D-122's 2^-116 reasoning; (3) `scripts/check-buildlog.py` + a fast-gate
leg — D-number contiguity, one row per number, four-column rows, balanced
code fences. It earned its place on its FIRST run: D-93's row carried
DUPLICATED trailing columns (why and artifacts repeated) from an old
truncated write — repaired.

Also fixed en route, found by the proofs: the JVM fixtures' subject id
was the literal string `"subject-1"` — not valid hex — and core correctly
refused it as a 16-byte envelope group id, silently failing every fixture
device's founding until the fixtures used realistic 32-hex subjects.

HONEST RESIDUE (details in §4): the lost-only-device question is the
founder's open decision; a two-key split is possible if two devices sign
in truly simultaneously (fails LOUD); a device that already received the
current key retains it until the sync key rotates; the agreement-keys
list is readable by any session of the account by design, and a revoked
device's registry binding persists until account deletion — the envelope
row is the enforcement point.

  invalidate the golden for no gain.

  sensitivity. For a value two shells must agree on byte-for-byte that
  is the D-122 lesson waiting to repeat, so D-124 pins one — derived
  independently in Python from the BIP-39 list before being asserted in
  Rust.
- **A phrase over the device id would have been useless.** It is over
  the KEY, which is what makes a substitution visible; the id is exactly
  what a substituting relay keeps constant.

- **Two governing documents disagreed and one of them said they did
  not.** `GUARANTEES.md` #5 read "Account is opt-in; sync is opt-in;

- **It was cheap to fix only because the repo is still private.** SPEC
  §121 calls breaking a guarantee a fork-worthy event; amending the
  wording before publication costs an edit, after publication it costs a
  promise. The window was open and is recorded as the reason for the
  timing.
- **The default lives in the ABSENCE of a key.** `sync/enabled` absent
  means ON, so default-on needs no migration and no backfill — every
  install predating the unit already behaves correctly. Only the literal
  byte `"0"` is off.
- **"No automatic pull exists" was verified, not assumed.** Every call
  site of `fireAndForget`/`ledgerChanged` and `restoreFromRelay` was
  read: the only automatic ledger traffic is the push hook, which is why
  gating it is sufficient. §4.3 carries the note so a future automatic
  pull is not added ungated.

  greyed-out sync switch or a dimmed Devices row shows a user without an
  account exactly what they are missing, which is the implication
  GUARANTEES #5 forbids. The twin tests pin absence, so a later "just
  disable it instead" cannot pass quietly.
- **The glyph carried a licence obligation.** lucide `user-round` is a
  FIFTH drawing and `NOTICE` said four. Upstream's geometry is unchanged
  (cx 12, cy 8, r 5); the circle is written as its arc path only because
  this builder takes path data rather than SVG `<circle>` elements.
- **iOS has no designed home shell, and this unit is where that stopped
  being invisible.** Android has `HomeShell` and a tab bar to hang a
  glyph on; iOS's root is `SmokeScreenView`, a developer menu. The
  screens are twins and the shells are not, so the entry point could not
  be a twin either. Recorded in §4.3 as the largest product gap on iOS
  rather than papered over with a second-best iOS entry point that would
  imply parity.

  sees it — which is why the fix is a grep in the gate rather than a
  test. The Recovery Kit read "Word 1 of 12: \(word)" to VoiceOver, on
  the one screen §3.4 calls "the only way back in".
- **The accent existed and no primary action used it.** Every call to
  action was `.buttonStyle(.bordered)`, so on the kit screen the single
  action carried the same weight as twelve grey word chips. That is what
  the founder reported as dated, and he was right; the light ground he
  did NOT complain about stays exactly as SPEC §11.1 chose it.

THE FINDINGS, recorded because they are the design:

- **SwiftUI's `tabItem` silently drops custom views.** A `Shape` placed
  there renders no icon and raises no error. The Lucide glyphs are
  rasterised to template images, and a test proves each raster contains
  ink — a blank square would otherwise pass unseen.
- **"Verbatim, not a redraw" needed a parser.** SwiftUI has no SVG path
  parser; SF Symbols would have been a different drawing and a broken
  NOTICE statement. The five glyphs' path strings were diffed against
  Android's `TabIcons.kt` programmatically: byte-identical. Arcs become
  cubic Béziers (W3C F.6.5) — encoding, not geometry — and NOTICE now
  says so.
- **D-127's sweep was blind to buttons with NO style.** It searched for
  `.buttonStyle(.bordered)`; five pressables had no style at all and read
  as plain steel text, including the Add tab's own action and Devices'
  approve. And `.disabled` does not dim a custom `ButtonStyle` — the style
  draws every pixel — which D-127 had papered over with a manual opacity
  on one button.
- **The blue placeholder was root-caused by falsification, on device.**
  (1) Styling the prompt with `.foregroundStyle`: no change, reverted.
  (2) The app shipped with no `AccentColor` and no global-accent build
  setting: true, fixed, verified in the compiled `Assets.car` and
  `NSAccentColorName` — and the placeholder stayed blue, so not the cause.
  (3) A string-literal title is a `LocalizedStringKey`; SwiftUI parses it
  as Markdown and autolinks an email address: `Text(verbatim:)` turned it
  grey. The sweep found no other such literal; a gate leg now refuses the
  class.
- **Three extraction traps, all in my own tooling.** XCTest writes the
  grand total as "Executed N tests, with 8 tests skipped and 0 failures":
  a pattern requiring "with N failures" never matched it, which is how
  D-126's and D-127's "13 + 5" (two class subtotals) reached the record —
  corrected in place. With one failure the line says "1 failure",
  singular, and a plural-only pattern grabbed a sub-suite's "8 tests"
  during sabotage run 4 — caught before recording. And counting
  `^run_gate` lines reported 6 legs because most legs are indented inside
  `if` blocks — caught before recording; the gate's own summary is the
  count.

Chosen to be deterministic: removing the sweep correction, or replacing curves with lines, can leave the circle's bounds unchanged and pass — a non-result |

  `unknown_kid_forces_a_refetch_once_the_key_set_rotates` opened with a token
  whose kid was not yet published. The key cache stores a fetched set only
  when it contains the requested kid, so that fetch cached nothing, and the
  "rotation" call that followed ran against an empty cache. The test passed
  without ever exercising the property its name claims — refetching past a
  WARM cache. Found by reading `key_for` while extracting it into `jwks.rs`.
  Corrected in place: a real sign-in warms the cache first. Sabotage S13
  (a warm cache never refetches) now turns it red, together with the new
  Google twin.
- **iOS's redirect is a documented ambiguity, not a settled fact.** Google's
  native-app OAuth page states custom URI schemes are unsupported "on Android
  and Chrome apps", and its redirect table still lists
  `com.googleusercontent.apps.123:/oauth2redirect`. A separate section says,
  with no platform named, that custom URI schemes are "no longer supported due
  to the risk of app impersonation". Google's own iOS SDK uses the reversed
  client id scheme, so it very likely works — but that is recorded as
  unproven until real client ids exist. If Google refuses, the fallbacks
  (Google's iOS SDK or AppAuth) break ADR-0035's "no new iOS dependency", so
  the choice goes to the founder.
- **My sabotage runner mislabelled every red row as a compile failure.** Its
  pattern `^error(\[E\d+\])?:` also matched cargo's "error: test failed, to
  rerun pass …", which `--no-fail-fast` prints whenever a test fails. Every
  row was re-evaluated from its saved log with the correct check
  (`error[E…]` or "could not compile", and three suites ran): no row had a
  compile error, and all twelve went red exactly as expected.

relay nonce on that basis. The first on-device ceremony (D-132, needing the Sign in with
Apple capability on the App ID) confirms it or sends it back.

THE FINDINGS:

- **The gap was ADR-0035's own wording, not a new idea.** Constraint 3 reads
  "on both platforms the relay verifies the ID token: … and a single-use nonce
  the relay issued". D-130 built that for Google and recorded Apple's absence
  as residue (e). Building the iOS Apple button first would have shipped the
  violation, so the relay change comes first and rides the same pending deploy.
- **The first full gate on this tree failed, 15 passed and 2 failed, and not on
  D-131's code.** `cargo audit` and `cargo deny` both flagged RUSTSEC-2026-0285
  (GHSA-2mjx-qc3c-rqvc), published the same day and after D-130's green gate:
  rustls 0.23.43, which the relay reaches through `ureq` 2.12.1, accepts TLS 1.3
  handshake messages across an encryption-level boundary. Every other leg of
  that run passed. `cargo update -p rustls` changed two lines of `Cargo.lock`
  (the version, 0.23.43 → 0.23.45, and its checksum) and nothing else; the dry
  run first confirmed no other crate would move. Audit then exited 0 and deny
  reported all four checks ok, before the gate below was run. Consequence
  recorded for the deploy: D-130's `04efa47` ships the vulnerable rustls, so
  the founder deploys this commit, not that one. The failing run is preserved
  under `scripts/gate-artifacts/20260914T19412*Z-*`.

- **A defaulted nonce keeps rejection uniform.** With a required field, axum's
  JSON extractor answers a request without a nonce with 422 and a different
  body: a second rejection shape on an auth route that promises one (D-27). The
  default makes it the same 401 `{}`, and a test pins that.
- **Separate stores, proven over HTTP, not assumed.** A relay booted with both
  providers issues a Google nonce; an Apple token carrying it is refused; the
  identical request with Apple's own nonce signs in.

- **My relay sabotage runner mis-attributed every failure.** cargo prints each
  "Running <binary>" line on stderr and the test results on stdout; the runner
  joined stdout before stderr, so no test line followed its binary's header
  and every failure read as binary "?". That matters here because
  `google_http` has a test with the same name as the A1 target. All five rows
  were re-derived from the saved logs: the k-th stdout "running N tests" block
  pairs with the k-th stderr "Running" line, an order confirmed on A1's log.
  Every row then matched. Two runner defects in two units (D-130's compile
  regex, this one) are the reason the verdict is always re-read from the logs.

  state use `SecRandomCopyBytes`. They are single-attempt protocol values, not
  keys, so D-66 does not apply.

  from or left in Safari's cookie jar, at the cost of retyping Google
  credentials at each sign-in.

evidence's `commit` is the HEAD at that moment, `f8f8cdd`. The commit adds only
