### 4.5 CI workflow vs the tree (audited 2026-08-25, pre-remote; first push landed 2026-08-25)

> **2026-08-27, CLOSED (D-106): CI reached `gate.sh --full` for the first time
> ever.** Every run since D-99 had died two steps earlier on a Kotlin-compiler
> path that cannot exist, silently — so every CI claim before this one
> described the workflow FILE and not a run. Run
> [33106530545](https://github.com/icrkdev/Skipti/actions/runs/33106530545) on
> PR #2 is the first that executed the gate and reported its own verdict:
>
> ```
> GATE PASSED WITH SKIPS — 12 passed, 1 skipped. Not a full green.
>   make ios-app   SKIPPED (Xcode or an iPhone simulator is unavailable)
> ```
>
> **Read that verdict literally, because the green check mark does not say
> it.** The JOB exits 0 — a skip is not a failure — while the GATE says 13/14
> (12/13 when this was first written, before D-108 added the fourteenth leg)
> and names the missing leg. Both are correct and the difference is the whole
> point of D-23's honest-skip rule: a Linux runner has no Xcode, so the iOS leg
> must SKIP rather than silently vanish or falsely pass. **A green CI badge on
> this repo therefore means 13/14, never 14/14**, and 14/14 exists only on a
> Mac with Xcode. **These numbers move every time a leg is added — if this
> sentence disagrees with a run, the run is right and this sentence is stale.** Anyone reading the badge as full coverage is reading it
> wrong; AGENTS.md §2 already says "GATE PASSED WITH SKIPS is not green" and
> that applies to CI exactly as it applies locally.
>
> What this run DID newly prove, which no local Mac gate can: the Android leg
> builds and packages on a clean Linux runner (`make android-app` BUILD
> SUCCESSFUL), the supply-chain legs pass with the pinned tooling, and the
> generated Kotlin bindings compile against the pinned compiler from the
> JetBrains distribution rather than Android Studio's bundled one.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` was audited before any remote existed so the
first push would not surprise. The push has since happened
(github.com/icrkdev/Skipti, private) and corrected the audit's own frame:
the discrepancies below could not "fire all at once on first push" because
the file was never valid YAML — the first run died in 0 s with zero jobs
started (incident §5.11, fixed by quoting one step name). The findings
below stand as recorded; resolving them per the recommendation remains open:

- **Tool installs are best-effort, the runs are not:** `cargo install
  cargo-{audit,deny,cyclonedx} || true` followed by unconditional
  `cargo audit` / `cargo deny check` / `cargo cyclonedx` steps. A failed
  install yields a confusing command-not-found failure instead of an
  honest skip — the opposite of D-23's principle and gate.sh's SKIP
  discipline.
- **CI does not know about half of what gate-full now checks:** no iOS
  leg (D-59 put `make ios-app` into gate-full) and no bindings-freshness
  check (D-43), so committed-but-stale bindings and a broken app build
  both pass CI green.
- **It reimplements the gate instead of calling it:** fmt, clippy,
  tests, the float audit and the release sweeps duplicate
  `scripts/gate.sh`'s legs as separate inline steps. gate.sh comments
  claim byte-for-byte alignment "on purpose", but nothing enforces it;
  the two already differ structurally (gate tallies test counts, CI
  prints raw output), and every future change to a leg must be made
  twice.
- **CI checks something the local gate never runs:** the SBOM step
  (`cargo cyclonedx`; `make sbom`) has no gate leg at all, so CI-green
  vs gate-full-green disagree in BOTH directions.
- **Trigger surface:** `on.push.branches: [main]` only — pushing current
  work-in-progress branches would run nothing even once a remote exists.

**Recommendation (recorded, deliberately NOT applied this session):**
CI should invoke `./scripts/gate.sh --full` as its primary verification
step, so CI and local can never disagree — the same reasoning D-43 used
for putting bindings freshness behind one shared command. Consequences
to settle when it lands: a Linux runner reports GATE PASSED WITH SKIPS
(iOS leg absent), which per AGENTS.md §2 is NOT green — either add a
macOS runner for a genuine 10/10 or publish the skip count as the honest
result; cache the installed audit tools (or use prebuilt binaries); and
decide whether SBOM stays CI-only or becomes a gate leg so the two
surfaces converge.
---

## 5. Incident log (bugs caught, kept for the record)

1. **GCM open() ignored seal()'s nonce prefix** — round-trip test caught it immediately; fixed by stripping/parsing the 12-byte prefix.
2. **`next_counter` did not advance state** — the 10⁷ harness detected duplicate nonces; fixed to mutate-and-return; harness now passes.
3. **Padding placed after the GCM tag** broke decryption; redesigned as inner, length-prefixed plaintext padding (D-17).
4. **Misremembered "published" GCM vector** failed its KAT; resolved by fetching official CAVP data and requiring independent OpenSSL agreement before pinning (D-15). Lesson encoded as policy: KAT constants enter the tree only via verified sources.
5. **`since=0` excluded record 0 and duplicates silently succeeded** — server semantics corrected (exclusive cursor, `409`) rather than bending tests to the bug.
6. **Flaky tampered-word test refused a commit** (caught by the gate during skrin work). BIP-39's checksum is 4 bits, so a single-word tamper on a *random* kit validated ~1/16 of runs. The checksum is transcription-error detection for humans, never an integrity control — the test wrongly leaned on its probability. Fixed by pinning fixture entropy; the generalisable lesson: a test that asserts a probabilistic property without pinning the draw is a latent gate-flaker.
6. **A-10's production floor was unpinned by any test** — external audit, 2026-08-24. `AUTH_RESPONSE_FLOOR` was 250 ms, but every timing test injected its own value via `new_shared_state_with_auth_floor`, and `new_shared_state()` — the constructor `main.rs` uses — was exercised by no test. Confirmed by experiment: setting the constant to `Duration::ZERO` left all 111 tests green with zero failing binaries, i.e. the anti-enumeration control could have been switched off in production without CI noticing. Fixed by pinning both the shipped value and its wiring, each verified to fail independently. Lesson, and it generalises past this one constant: **a control tested only through an injection seam is untested in the configuration that ships.** Where a test injects a value, something must also assert the production default.
7. **A-12 asserted only failures** — same audit. The revocation test checked that the revoked device could not unwrap five envelope rows, but never established that its key material worked at all, so a malformed row or broken agreement key would have satisfied it for the wrong reason. Fixed with a positive control: d3 opens its own epoch-0 envelope and recovers exactly the shared key before revocation. `escrow_http.rs` already had this shape and was the model.
8. **Group envelopes were never persisted** — caught by the first run of the restart-survival suite, 2026-08-24. The vault had `replace_group_envelopes` and boot called `load_envelopes`, but `envelope_push` — the only writer — called neither: envelopes lived memory-only while every other MUST-persist category had its write-through wired. Exactly the failure shape ADR-0024's proof exists for: the pre-restart positive control read back fine, so only the reopen exposed the empty set (`left: "[]"`). Fixed by wiring the full-set replace into the handler; removing the write-through again fails the test at that exact assertion (verified via stash). Lesson, generalising §5.6's: **a trait method nobody calls is dead code wearing a load-bearing name** — every boot-side loader must have a live-side writer in the same category, and the proof suite is what pairs them.
9. **The Xcode project file had a duplicate object ID, committed HEAD did not build for tests, and a logged test suite had never once executed** — found while wiring passkeys (D-57), 2026-08-25. `A10026` was defined twice (SyncE2ETests-in-Sources and SyncService-in-Sources); resolution order decided which file landed where, and in NO resolution did both land correctly: xcodebuild resolved it to SyncE2ETests.swift inside the APP target, where XCTest is unresolvable — `make ios-app` failed outright on committed HEAD (the fast Rust gate cannot see any of this) — while SyncService compiled nowhere and the test-target phase never listed SyncE2ETests at all, so its three tests had silently never run. Verified both halves today: the failing build before the fix, and 27/27 with zero skips after it, sync E2E included, against a live relay. Lesson: **an iOS claim without a fresh `make ios-app` is a hypothesis** — the same lesson as this log's standing warning about tree-vs-document, but for the half of the repo `make gate` does not reach.
10. **The fresh-install vault path was a race, and the failure screenshot
    went uncommitted** — found completing D-58's bundle-id verification,
    2026-08-25. The prior session committed the SUCCESS screenshot of the
    first launch under `com.vardrlabs.skipti` and left the FAILURE
    untracked (`bundle-id-fresh-install.png`, 18:08): a fresh-install
    attempt dying on `Sqlite("table hlc_state already exists")`. Root
    cause: `SkiptiApp.loadGate` and the balance screen both opened the
    vault on concurrent queues; on a fresh file both could pass the
    `user_version` check before either committed the schema (and two
    first-opens could provision competing Keychain keys). The 17:51
    success was the race won — §5.9's "an iOS claim without a fresh run is
    a hypothesis", one level up: timing cherry-picked the evidence, and
    the honest artifact was the one that did not get committed. Fixed
    structurally (D-60: one process-wide open gate; the gate no longer
    opens the vault at all on verification paths) and proven by the
    previously-flaky cycle now running three times byte-identical plus a
    relaunch. Lesson: **when a verification produces both a success and a
    failure artifact, the failure is the finding** — commit it, diagnose
    it, and only then claim the path works.

11. **CI was never valid YAML — the first push proved it could not fire at
    all** — github.com/icrkdev/Skipti (private) went live 2026-08-25 at
    commit fbed158. §4.5 had audited the workflow pre-push and predicted
    its discrepancies would "fire all at once on first push"; the reality
    was sharper: the first run failed in 0 seconds with NO jobs started.
    Line 23 read `- name: Float audit (ADR-0002: no f32/f64 ...)` — an
    unquoted colon-space, which YAML parses as a nested mapping, killing
    the whole file at parse time. Fixed by quoting the step name. Lesson,
    sharpening §4.5: **a config file that has never executed is a
    hypothesis, exactly like an iOS claim without a fresh
    `make ios-app`** — a static audit catches drift against the tree but
    cannot catch parse-level death; only execution is evidence.

12. **Envelope pushes silently diverged from the vault on repeat** — caught
    by the deletion suite's first run, 2026-08-26. `r_envelopes`'s PRIMARY
    KEY is (group_id, recipient_device_id), so the write-through's INSERT OR
    REPLACE collapsed a second push FOR the same recipient into their first
    row — while the in-memory slot happily kept both. ADR-0024 promises
    vault and memory identical; for any group where a member pushed twice,
    they were NOT, and only a reopen exposed it (`left: "[]"` shaped — one
    row instead of two). No test had ever pushed twice to one recipient.
    Fixed by making both push paths upsert-by-recipient (one current wrapped
    blob per recipient — which is also what D-37 rotation semantics want),
    with /replace keeping its wholesale-authoritative shape (a first fix
    attempt broke A-12's read leg and was itself caught by the suite within
    minutes: upserting a replacement set must still REMOVE absent
    recipients). Regression test in relay.rs proves memory == vault across a
    real close/reopen. Lesson: **the store's primary keys are part of the
    protocol's type system** — memory structures must be normalised to them,
    or the persistence boundary becomes a silent projection that only
    restarts can see.

13. **A byte-pinned assertion over JSONEncoder output flaked across iOS
    suite runs** — same session, runs at 00:06–00:12 UTC today.
    The Apple sign-in stub test asserted the request body as an exact
    string; Foundation's JSONEncoder does not guarantee key order, so the
    identical code failed one full-suite run, passed the next, failed under
    -only-testing. Diagnosed from the xcresult (actual body showed
    sync_device_id FIRST), fixed by asserting the decoded key→value mapping.
    This is §5.6's lesson extended one step: **an assertion over output the
    platform leaves unspecified is a coin flip wearing a test's clothes** —
    pin inputs and mappings, never incidental serialisation order.

14. **SECURITY.md published a vulnerability-reporting address on a domain
    nobody owns** — found 2026-08-26 while preparing public-facing files
    for review. SECURITY.md directed reports to security@skipti.app with a
    PGP key at https://skipti.app/security/pgp.txt; `dig NS skipti.app`
    answers empty — the domain is UNREGISTERED. While the repo is private,
    reports bounce and SPEC Phase 8's working-disclosure-contact
    requirement is unmet by that file; when the repo goes public, anyone
    can register skipti.app and silently receive security disclosures for
    an end-to-end encrypted finance app, encrypting them to an
    attacker-chosen key. Fixed same session: reporting address moved to
    security@vardrlabs.com (MX verified live, smtp.google.com); the PGP
    line dropped entirely rather than repointed — no PGP key exists yet,
    and GitHub security advisories (already offered in the same file) are
    an adequate encrypted channel until one does. The repo-wide sweep of
    every outbound URL/email in README/NOTICE/CONTRIBUTING/GUARANTEES/
    THREAT_MODEL found no other occurrence (ADR-0026 names skipti.app
    twice as a REJECTED alternative in superseded reasoning — decision-
    record prose, not a published endpoint). Lesson, generalising past
    this file: **a published contact for a domain you do not control is
    worse than no contact** — it launders attacker-controlled infrastructure
    with the project's own authority, so every outbound URL in any
    public-facing document must resolve to a host the project actually
    holds. If skipti.app is ever registered, moving the address back is a
    deliberate, separate change — not assumed here.

15. **Foundation strips a leading UTF-8 BOM from `String(bytes:encoding:)` —
    a BOM-prefixed CSV cannot survive the UniFFI→Swift lift** — found
    2026-08-26 while proving the flat CSV export over the FFI. The Rust
    writer emitted the §9.2 BOM as the first bytes of its output; Rust tests
    asserted it; the Swift test received text starting at "record_type" with
    no U+FEFF. Isolated reproduction: `[0xEF,0xBB,0xBF,0x72,0x65]` decoded
    with `String.Encoding.utf8` yields scalars `[114,101]` — Foundation
    treats a LEADING BOM as an encoding signature, not content. Mid-string
    BOMs survive (proven by a marker experiment), and JSON's leading `{`
    survives, so the loss is specific to position 0. Kotlin's lift keeps
    the BOM — meaning one core function would have returned
    platform-divergent strings from the same bytes, the worst kind of
    boundary drift. Fix: `write_csv` is pure RFC 4180 text (the RFC itself
    specifies no BOM); §9.2's "UTF-8 with BOM for Excel" becomes the file
    WRITER'S job in each shell, while `parse_csv` still tolerates
    BOM-carrying input because real Splitwise exports carry one. En route,
    flip-flopping evidence (the same test failing then passing without an
    intervening change) traced to a stale incremental test bundle — a clean
    DerivedData settled it; D-59's lesson applied twice in one session.
    Lesson: **a string invariant that crosses a platform boundary must be
    proven AT the platform boundary** — Rust-side assertions cannot see
    what Foundation does to the bytes on arrival.

16. **Two sessions converged on one working tree, and the collision was
    caught by cross-checking both survivors' claims** — 2026-08-26 evening,
    during the schema-migration and Android-pipeline work. A glitched second
    opencode session ran concurrently with this one (evidence, not inference:
    file mtimes advancing between reads inside a single turn, an unattributed
    commit landing mid-session at a38bce8's timestamp, `core/Cargo.toml`
    modified between two greps of it). Neither writer clobbered the other to
    unbuildable state only because each verified rather than assumed: when
    jsonio.rs arrived containing BOTH sessions' v1 implementations, the union
    was reconciled by testing which fixture actually byte-matched the pin —
    this session's hand-derived fixture carried THREE duplicated hex pairs
    (34-char ids that fail validation) while the twin's inline FIXTURE_V1 was
    exact, so the twin's won and the broken artifact was deleted. The same
    rule resolved staging anomalies (`git add` nobody ran) and one
    sentence-level contradiction (commit message says jna 5.19.0, tree pins
    5.19.1). Lesson for future multi-operator reality: **when the tree moves
    under you, stop writing and diff; never merge by assumption** — and
    afterwards the DOUBLED check is what made salvage legal (my gradle APK
    proof forced `cargo clean` + rebuild so its artifacts were provably
    THIS session's compile, plus Gradle's FROM-CACHE restore is hash-keyed,
    making cache-hits cryptographic equivalences rather than staleness).

17. **Generated bindings were proven byte-current but never BUILDABLE** —
    generalised from D-91's Android find, 2026-08-27. The freshness gate
    regenerates and byte-diffs both binding trees, which passed cleanly the
    entire time the committed Kotlin had never once been compiled anywhere;
    Swift only escaped by luck of adjacency — the iOS app consumed it, so a
    compile error would have surfaced there (D-59's leg), while Kotlin's
    error surfaced only when Android arrived to consume it. Lesson: **a
    diff proves identity with what WOULD be generated; only a compiler
    proves it was ever valid.** Closed structurally (D-94): the gate leg
    compiles the Kotlin tree standalone wherever a JDK+kotlinc exists,
    independent of any SDK.

18. **The iOS gate leg failed spuriously, and nothing could say why** —
    founder-reported exit 2 on `make ios-app` at unchanged HEAD, green on
    re-run and standalone, no log retained because the leg reported only an
    exit code. Mechanism aligned with the one recorded observation of its
    family (the dropped LedgerPort test inside a parallel simulator clone):
    Xcode 26 parallelises tests onto clones of an AUTOGENERATED scheme even
    when the repo pins no such preference, and a clone can silently drop
    work. Re-priced on measurement rather than superstition: clone
    parallelism saves ~0 s here (§3's A/B), so serialisation is pinned
    explicitly and full failing output is preserved at two layers from now
    on (D-93). Unrepentantly narrow claim kept honest: this exact failure
    cannot be reproduced or attributed after the fact; what IS claimed is
    the elimination of the only caught mechanism plus mandatory evidence on
    any future occurrence.

19. **The flake fix that measured the wrong variable** — 2026-08-27. After
    D-93's serialisation landed, `make ios-app` STILL failed ~half of ten
    runs, identically signed (`SBMainWorkspace … Busy`). D-93's A/B (29.1 s
    parallel vs 29.3 s serial) had "proven" clones cost nothing — true, and
    irrelevant: it timed EXECUTION cost while the failure lived in device
    LIFECYCLE. The founder's three falsifications (clone pin, install wipe,
    daemon restart) plus this session's fourth (30-second spacing still
    2F/3) bracketed the space until boot-once-UDID-reuse went 8/8 where
    name=-resolution went ~50/50 under identical commands — one variable
    left standing (D-96). Lesson generalised with D-93 as its exhibit:
    **an A/B proves only what it varies; check that the varied knob
    plausibly touches the failing operation before citing equivalence as
    exoneration.** With preserved logs, falsification took minutes, not
    sessions.

20. **Passkey enrolment authenticated nobody — pre-auth account takeover**
    (D-102). `POST /v1/auth/passkey/register/start` accepted an identifier
    from the request body with no bearer, and `register/finish` stored its
    challenge under `challenge_id` alone with no identifier beside it. Either
    hole alone is sufficient. An unauthenticated caller enrolled its own
    authenticator against any address and then signed in as that account —
    reaching the victim's ciphertext bucket, their escrow blob (the wrapped
    MK, which turns escrow into an offline passphrase problem), and account
    deletion. Found by reading the two finish paths SIDE BY SIDE:
    `authenticate_finish` returned the identifier its challenge was issued
    for, `register_finish` took one as an argument. The asymmetry WAS the
    bug, and it was visible in forty lines of the same file.

    Proven before it was fixed, with a real software authenticator rather
    than by argument: register/finish 200 for an unowned identifier, a
    challenge started for `attacker@` finished for `victim@`, and a live
    access token for a subject nobody proved. Then fixed at both halves and
    sabotage-tested at both halves independently.

    **Lesson, and it is not "add a bearer".** Sign-in and enrolment sat in
    one file, four adjacent routes, one mental category — "the passkey
    surface" — and the category hid that two of them ASSERT identity while
    two CONSUME it. Routes that mint identity and routes that require it are
    not the same surface however adjacent their code. The relay's own router
    now says so structurally: enrolment is grouped with revocation and
    deletion behind the bearer gate, not with the sign-in routes it used to
    sit among.

    Every other guard here held while this one did not: buckets stayed
    subject-scoped, envelopes device-scoped, escrow subject-scoped, timing
    floored. That is the shape of the finding — not a weak system, one
    unchecked door in a strong one, which is exactly the door an audit is
    for.

21. **The connection limiter's own `verify` carried an unfalsifiable line —
    caught on its first live run** (ADR-0032 layer 1, §4.4's written-not-run
    gap closing exactly as predicted). The founder ran `apply && verify` on
    the box. Everything load-bearing passed: the DROP landed at position 1,
    above the `dpt:443` ACCEPT at position 7, and `0 LOG targets in INPUT`.
    The last line said `(no counter line yet — the rule has never matched)`.

    It was not reporting a fact. The counter check grepped for `$NAME`
    (`skipti443`), which is the **/proc table name** and never appears in
    `iptables -L` output — the founder's own position line proves it, showing
    `limit: above 20/min burst 40 mode srcip htable-max 8192` and no name at
    all. So that grep could not match on a working rule: it would have printed
    "the rule has never matched" forever, whatever the counters said, and a
    future operator checking whether the limiter was doing anything would have
    been told "no" by a line that knew nothing.

    Benign — it gates nothing — and still the same defect class as §5.20's
    fix and D-103's first tests: **a check that cannot fail**. Third instance
    in one session, which is the argument for treating it as a habit rather
    than a lesson. Now matches what iptables actually prints
    (`dpt:443.*limit: above`), tested against the founder's verbatim output in
    both `-L` and `-L -v` shapes, and it EXITS NON-ZERO when the rule is
    absent rather than printing a reassuring sentence.

    **Two honest limits surfaced with it, now in ADR-0032 as tripwires.**
    (1) `/proc/net/ipt_hashlimit/<name>` is readable and lists the source
    addresses being counted. That is not persistence — ephemeral kernel
    memory, expiring on its own, nothing writes it down — so §2.6's analysis
    stands. But "written nowhere" was too comfortable: there IS a readable
    view, and anything that `cat`s it to a terminal or scrapes it on a timer
    converts an expiring counter into a log of client addresses. `verify`
    deliberately does not print it and says why in-line. (2) The budget is per
    source address, so everyone behind a carrier NAT shares one — fine at
    pre-release scale, not fine at scale, and the first symptom will be a
    support report rather than a metric, because the metric would need the
    addresses.

22. **An audit commit swept another agent's in-flight work under its own
    message** — §5.16's pattern, second occurrence, and this time the audit
    was the offender. Commit `b2593cd`, whose message is "Fix an unfalsifiable
    line in the connection limiter's own verify", carries three files that
    belong to it and **fourteen that do not**: the entire D-107 Android
    balance screen — `BalanceScreen.kt` (376 lines), `BalanceFixtures.kt`,
    `AppLocale.kt`, `BalanceScreenTest.kt`, a `build.gradle.kts` dependency,
    and five screenshots. Cause: `git add -A` while a second agent had
    uncommitted work in the tree.

    Ox Alpha caught it, reported it rather than building on it (which is what
    §5.16 asks for and is the reason this is a clean recovery rather than a
    tangle), recorded the real decision separately in `65338c2`, and left the
    call on rewriting to the party that owns git. Correct on every count.

    **Not rewritten, deliberately.** `b2593cd` was already pushed and CI had
    run on it, and force-pushing `main` to tidy a message would destroy the
    record of the mistake — which is precisely the move this project does not
    make. The BUILD-LOG discipline is "corrected in place, never quietly
    rewritten" (D-96 is the exemplar), and history deserves the same
    treatment: `65338c2`'s subject names the sweep, and this entry is the
    correction. The cost is real and accepted — anyone reading `b2593cd`
    alone is misled, and only the next commit and this entry undeceive them.

    **The durable fix is not "be careful", it is where the rule lives.**
    "Never two writers at once" existed only in the founder's handoff
    document, which lives OUTSIDE the repo and which only one of the two
    agents reads. A rule that binds two parties cannot sit in a file one of
    them never opens. `AGENTS.md` §4 — auto-loaded, read by both — now
    carries it as a concrete instruction ("stage explicit paths; never
    `git add -A`") rather than a principle, because the principle was already
    understood by everyone and stopped nothing.

    **A second hole, exposed by the very commit that fixed the first.**
    Staging `AGENTS.md`, `Makefile`, `scripts/gate.sh` and this file made the
    pre-commit hook announce *"no Rust files staged — skipping the gate
    (docs-only commit)"*. It was not a docs-only commit: it changed the gate
    itself. The trigger was `.rs` / `Cargo.*` / `deny.toml`, so **the one file
    whose breakage makes every future gate meaningless was the one file exempt
    from the gate** — a commit that broke `scripts/gate.sh` would have sailed
    through announcing itself as documentation. `Makefile`, `scripts/gate.sh`
    and the hook itself now trigger it (running the gate is also the cheapest
    possible check that the gate still runs), and the message no longer claims
    "docs-only" about commits that are nothing of the sort. Kotlin and Swift
    stay off the list deliberately: the FAST gate is Rust-only and would not
    check them either way, and `--full` is too slow for a hook. Proven live —
    the commit carrying this fix is the first to trip its own new trigger.

    **And a third, in the same five minutes.** The BUILD-LOG edit recording
    that fix asserted an anchor that did not exist, so `buildlog_edit.py`
    refused it — correctly, that is exactly what D-52 built it for — but the
    commit went ahead anyway with a message claiming "recorded as the second
    half of §5.22" when nothing had been recorded. Caught by reading the
    command's own output instead of assuming it worked, and amended before
    pushing. The lesson is small and keeps recurring in this session: **a
    tool that refuses loudly still needs someone to read the refusal.**

23. **THE D-102 FIX WAS NEVER DEPLOYED — the pre-auth account takeover is
    LIVE on production, and a test was asserting that it should be.** Found
    while auditing D-117's "relay-up gate finding".

    D-117 reported that the iOS leg fails when a relay is reachable, because
    `register/start` is driven bearerless and takes D-102's 401. The mechanism
    was exactly right; the relay was not `:8080` but **production**:

    ```
    GET  /version                                     -> be4bba5f7e1a… (2026-08-26)
    POST /v1/auth/passkey/register/start  (no bearer) -> 200
    ```

    `be4bba5` is an ANCESTOR of `004bd0e`, D-102's fix. Production has not
    been redeployed since the day before the takeover was found, is 58
    commits behind `main` (3 touching `server/`), and answers 200 to exactly
    the request that defines the vulnerability. Anyone can enrol a passkey
    against any identifier on `skipti.vardrlabs.com` right now.

    Stated rather than assumed: the instance has no real users yet, so the
    live risk is PRE-REGISTRATION — an attacker enrolling a credential
    against an address a future user will sign up with, and holding it. That
    survives the deploy unless `r_passkeys` is checked afterwards.

    **The test was worse than absent.** `testRegisterStartServesTheProductionRpId`
    asserted `status == 200` and read the served `rp.id`. Written before
    D-102, it encoded the vulnerable behaviour as expected. It was green only
    BECAUSE production was unpatched, and it would have turned RED on the
    deploy that fixed the vulnerability — presenting the security deploy as
    the thing that broke the gate. A test that fails when you close a security
    hole is worse than one that does not exist.

    Rewritten as `testRegisterStartRefusesWithoutASession`, asserting D-102's
    contract (401, uniform empty body) with a failure message naming the
    remedy. **The full gate is RED right now, on exactly one leg, for a true
    reason, and goes green on the deploy.** CI is unaffected — the iOS leg
    skips on Linux — which is itself worth noting: this class of finding is
    invisible to CI by construction.

    Cost recorded: the served `rp.id` is no longer assertable live, since
    obtaining it needs a session and the relay never exposes an OTP code. The
    host binding is still covered by `testAasaAuthorisesThisApp` and ADR-0027;
    recovering the served value lands with the authenticated passkey unit.

    **The audit's own miss, which is why this sat for a day.** D-102's record
    claims "no client regressed: `PasskeyAuthService.startRegistration` is
    wired to NO screen". That was checked against SCREENS, not against TESTS,
    and a live test was calling the route. Changing a route's auth contract
    means auditing every caller, and a test is a caller. Ox Alpha found it;
    the audit shipped it.


    **CLOSED 2026-08-28, verified independently.** The founder deployed
    `69aeb87`. Probed from outside rather than read from a report:

    ```
    /version                                      -> 69aeb87e669c... == local HEAD
    POST /v1/auth/passkey/register/start   (bare) -> 401
    POST /v1/auth/passkey/register/finish  (bare) -> 401
    POST /v1/auth/passkey/authenticate/start      -> 401
    POST /v1/auth/otp/request                     -> 200
    SELECT identifier FROM r_passkeys             -> (empty)
    ```

    The empty credential table is the part that matters beyond the patch:
    **nothing was pre-registered during the window**, so no credential
    outlived the fix. The pre-registration risk named above did not
    materialise.

    And the full gate went green ON ITS OWN. The iOS leg passes because it
    asks the REAL relay, so green here means the fix is live rather than
    merely merged — the one thing no local test could have told us. The red
    gate cleared itself the moment production was correct, which is what a
    test pointed at production is for.

    **One inaccuracy found while probing, worth a line.** D-65 records that a
    dev-mint probe on a default build "answers axum's ordinary 404". It
    answers **401** — and so does every unmatched route (`/nope`,
    `/v1/definitely/not/a/route`), so the mechanism is a blanket-401
    fallback, not anything route-specific. The SECURITY property D-65 was
    protecting is intact, and it is what the live test actually asserts:
    `testDevMintIsAbsentFromProduction` compares the dev path against a
    nonsense path and demands equal status AND byte-identical bodies. It pins
    INDISTINGUISHABILITY rather than a particular code, which is why it
    stayed green and why it was right to. Only the prose is wrong.

24. **A decision row was silently dropped from BUILD-LOG and went unnoticed
    for five units** — external audit, 2026-08-31, found while auditing D-122.
    The table held 121 rows numbered 1..122: **D-55 was missing.** Not
    renumbered, not superseded — gone, while D-56, D-57, D-65, D-117 and D-120
    all still cite it in prose ("`RelayHTTPRequest.bearer` existed since
    D-55"), so the log referenced a record it no longer contained. Bisected to
    `b7f2df8` (the D-117 unit): present at its parent, absent at that commit
    and every commit after. Restored verbatim from `3641d21`.
    **This is the third occurrence of the class `scripts/buildlog_edit.py`
    exists to prevent** (the first two — changelog (12), evidence blocks
    D-49/D-50 — are why it was written in D-52), which is the finding: the
    tool only helps on the edit that uses it, and nothing verifies the
    document afterwards. The drop survived four cold audits, including two of
    mine, because every audit read the rows that were THERE. Lesson, and it
    generalises past this row: **an anchored-edit tool prevents the edit that
    drops content; it does not detect content already dropped.** A structural
    check is cheap and belongs in the gate — D-number contiguity, one row per
    number, every row well-formed, code fences balanced. Recorded as owed in
    §4; the audit ran it by hand this time.

25. **A WORKLOG-only commit deleted 98 files** — D-192, 2026-10-01, found by
    Claude one commit later. Commit `0ed4d0e` ("WORKLOG: D-192 built,
    uncommitted…") staged `docs/WORKLOG.md` by explicit path, as the rule
    says. But the unit's deletions had been made with `git rm`, which stages
    them, so the index already held 98 deletions (both shells' relay files
    and tests, the `server/` crate) and the commit carried them under a
    WORKLOG message; it was pushed. main at `0ed4d0e` and `c63d1ae` does not
    build (the remaining files still referenced the deleted ones) until the
    D-192 code commit `27cb6a2`. Not rewritten (that needs a force-push);
    `c63d1ae` and this entry say what happened. Lesson: **explicit paths
    control what you ADD, not what is already staged.** `git diff --cached
    --stat` before every commit, including a docs-only one.

26. **Unreleased builds ran online on two devices signed in to production** — D-211, 2026-10-14, the
    controller's mistake (Claude). To look at screens, the controller let subagents launch the
    unreleased D-211 build on the AVD `skipti-shots` (signed in to the founder's account) and on the
    iOS 27 simulator AFAF4221 (the gate's default, signed in to Test Vard), against PRODUCTION. On
    Android the test photo was set in airplane mode and the vault restored before going online, but
    the build also ran online twice. Verified read-only with gcloud the same day: production holds
    41 records, the newest 2026-10-13T20:30Z, none written on the 14th; ONE write landed: Test Vard's
    `users/{uid}.name` at 19:25:45Z (the new ensure-name step; 9 characters, almost certainly its
    own name). Nothing else. Fixed: looks only on throwaway devices against the local emulators
    (memory `skipti-looks-throwaway-devices`); an XCTest host starts no cloud work and has no real
    account (D-211 fix 2/3), because hosted tests run the app on clones of that simulator.
    Lesson: **a look device that is signed in to production is production.** A dispatch names the
    throwaway device it may use; anything else is forbidden.
27. **Both export proofs failed on main for a day with every gate green**: D-211, 2026-10-14, found
    in D-215 on 2026-10-15; the controller's mistake (Claude). D-211 moved the export to schema 4 and
    left both proof surfaces checking the old prefix `"schema_version":3,` (iOS
    ExportProofScreen.swift, Android Exporter.kt), so `--export-proof` printed PROOF FAILED on three
    JSON checks on both shells. No test ran either proof, so the gate could not see it; the founder
    did. Fixed in D-215 P1 (013d4ca):
    the prefix follows the schema constant, and a test on each shell runs the proof itself
    (`ExportFlowTests.testTheExportProofPasses`, `PortTest.the_export_proof_passes_row_by_row`).
    Lesson: **a proof surface nobody runs is a claim, not a proof.** Every proof arg gets a test
    that runs it.
28. **An agent stashed the shared tree while another agent's edits were in flight**: D-217,
    2026-10-16, a near miss; the controller's process gap (Claude). Two subagents worked one
    checkout in parallel on disjoint files (Task 5 iOS, Task 4 Android); the iOS agent ran
    `git stash; git stash apply`, which swept the Android agent's uncommitted edits into the
    stash and back. Nothing was lost (checked the same hour: an empty stash list, both commits
    holding exactly their own files), but one failed apply would have lost another agent's work.
    Fixed: CLAUDE.md section 4 "Speed rules" item 4 and memory `skipti-parallel-agents-shared-tree`:
    parallel agents in one checkout never stash, reset, checkout or restore, each refuses to
    commit with a file it did not stage, and the controller dispatches a committing agent only
    on an empty index. Lesson: **a whole-tree git command in a shared tree is another agent's
    undo button.**
29. **The run's build caches filled the disk and stopped a look**: D-225, 2026-10-17; the controller's process gap
    (Claude). The session 5 run kept every look's and sabotage lane's DerivedData from D-219 to D-224 (about 31 GB under
    `/private/tmp/skipti-d2xx-*-dd` and `.drafts/*/dd`), and the data volume fell to 5.7 GB free of 460. During D-225
    Task 3 the Android emulator refused to boot ("Not enough space to create userdata partition", also with the data
    partition lowered to 2 GB and 800 MB), so the task could not take its look and was held uncommitted. The agent
    deleted nothing and stopped; the founder approved deleting the old caches, 53 GB came free, and Task 3 looked and
    committed (0343a2c). Nothing was lost. Fixed: CLAUDE.md section 4's clean-up rule (2afedef, the founder's) and
    `.superpowers/sdd/run-common.md`: every unit's close-out deletes that unit's throwaway build products right after
    the push (DerivedData and build directories of looks and sabotage lanes, leftover worktrees, throwaway devices),
    keeps every piece of evidence, never touches the gate's shared build directories or the founder's devices, and
    checks free space before a gate or look (under 30 GB, clean first); every agent deletes its own build products when
    it finishes. Lesson: **a build cache nobody owns is a disk nobody can use.**
30. **The app lock failed open for one commit on the D-232 branch**: D-232, 2026-10-19, a near miss; the implementer's
    miss (Claude), caught by the confirmation review, never merged. Decision 78 makes Android 12+ re-create the activity
    when the app tells the system a new night mode, and the lock locked on every re-creation (rotation already did, at
    any timeout: a fail-closed bug since the lock existed). The fix, a0e7a34, let a re-created activity keep the lock's
    state. Read-only review traced the pure rules by hand and found the hole (C1, Critical): an activity re-created
    BEFORE the process's first launch decision kept `locked = false`, so the ledger opened without the lock. Two ways
    in: anyone holding the unlocked phone rotates it at once while SKIPTI opens, and, with no one trying, the first
    D-232 launch of every upgraded Android 12+ install with the lock on whose mode differs from the phone's. The test
    table had no row for that order. 69a5780 fixed it the same hour (`launchDecided`: a fresh process starts undecided
    and decides, so it fails closed; sabotage row L7), and 2e2adc8 closed the one residual the second confirmation
    found (h1: the in-front mark expires after 2 s, sabotage row L8). The lock look on API 34 and 37 then locked every
    C1 case on a device. Nothing was released or merged with the hole; the only build that carried it
    was the decision 78 re-look's throwaway emulator (built at a0e7a34). Lesson: **a fix that lets a
    security control skip its own decision needs the row where nothing has decided yet.**
31. **An index race put another agent's staged core file into a Firebase commit**: D-235, 2026-10-19, the core
    implementer's miss (Claude), owned in its report (`wave-a-report.md` 6). Wave A's round 3 implementer staged
    `core/src/straumr/mod.rs` (the era tests and a simpler receive) in the shared checkout; in the second between its
    `git add` and its `git commit`, the wave B implementer committed its round 2, and the whole index went with it, so
    814fe02 ("D-235 wave B round 2: the log read per author, never refused ...") carries that core file. The content
    was correct and gated (the hook's fast gate passed, and wave A's later sabotage rows, its confirmation and the
    whole-branch review read it), but the commit's message does not describe it; 85e7de9's message records where the
    change went, and history is not rewritten. The wave A agent had printed `git diff --cached --name-only`, which
    listed wave B's staged files, and committed without gating on it. Every later D-235 commit named its paths
    (`git commit -- <paths>`) after checking the index held nothing else. Lesson: **in a shared checkout a commit
    names its paths; a bare `git commit` after `git add` commits whatever anyone staged.**

## 6. Update protocol

After finishing each phase: re-run §3 commands, reconcile §1/§4 against reality,
append dated notes below, and only then claim progress. Claims without a
reproducing command belong in §4, not §1.

  creation through core's tick/receive rules over the FFI — an offline
  device's records slot into their timestamp position on reconnect. The
  founder's scenario is a test on both shells: three devices, one
  account, interleaved writes, one offline throughout — identical record
  sets, identical projections, identical money, NOTHING lost. The
  loss-path regression fails on the snapshot engine by construction.

  and LWW edits named in §4. Sabotage: merge removed, cursor frozen,
  rebuild removed (Android), merge removed, seal skipped (iOS) — each

  checked the hex string and could not fail). Full gate 14/14, 108 JVM
  tests (216 executions), iOS 0 failures. (Tally corrected D-122: the

- **2026-08-29 (2)** — Record-level sync (D-121, ADR-0034's first
- **2026-08-31** — D-122: the three silent-loss paths D-121's promise
  still hid, all three reproduced before fixing. (1) Both MemoryRelay
  stubs stored the log as a LIST and only checked collisions against
  already-stored entries — a batch carrying the same index twice was
  accepted by the stub and refused by the real relay, which is exactly
  what excused (2): every record in a multi-record push bore the SAME
  log index (nextIndex() is a pure cursor read, called per record) —
  N pending records meant N entries at one index, 409 after 409, the
  first record stored again on every retry and the rest stranded
  offline. Fixed on both shells: base+i per batch, the server's
  authoritative next_index preferred over the client-computed one, and
  the 409 reconcile now reuses pullAndMerge's pull instead of issuing a
  second one. (3) iOS read the persisted HLC counter from the FIRST
  four bytes (the top of millis — 0 below 2^32, a constant 416 at
  production magnitude), collapsing every same-millisecond record onto
  one identity, which skrin v2's UNIQUE index then turned into silent
  local destruction — three iOS call sites now decode through ONE
  decodeHlcState helper. (4) a pre-D-121 vault (kv-only rows, zero
  records) lost its ENTIRE ledger on the first pull — the projection
  rebuild overwrites the kv rows from the record path — fixed with a
  one-time idempotent backfill minting records from the legacy rows at
  the top of every pull, on both shells. New proofs on both shells: the
  multi-record push (N records, N distinct indices, 409-retry loses
  nothing), three same-millisecond records keep distinct identities
  (pinned at production magnitude — two could never fail), the HLC
  codec golden at production magnitude (iOS), and the upgrade test
  (kv-only vault survives the pull, becomes pushable). Sabotage: index
  fix reverted → multi-record red; iOS offset reverted → exactly the
  codec golden + same-millis red; backfill removed → upgrade red; stub
  reverted to a list → the multi-record test STILL red (the
  distinct-index assertion catches the bug even through the lenient
  stub — stronger than the paste predicted). BUILD-LOG corrections:
  D-121's JVM tally was 216 executions = 108 x 2 (RecordSyncTest 6),
  not 214 = 107 x 2; SyncProof.kt removed from D-121's artifact list;
  the truncated D-119 changelog fragment repaired. Latent note: the
  constant nonce sessions on record factories are safe only because no
  record is ever sealed through straumr::seal_record — commented at
  both sites. One unexplained single-occurrence JVM flake recorded in
  §4.3. Full gate 14/14, 0 skipped.

- **2026-09-01** — D-123: the account's devices share one sync key. The
  founder's mechanism: a new device is authorised by an EXISTING device —
  X25519 agreement keypairs, the sync key wrapped to the new device's
  published public key through the EXISTING envelope path (the account's
  device set is a group; the same mechanism as group keys, D-37). Core
  gains ffiDeviceAgreementGenerate + ffiSyncKeyWrap/Unwrap (subject id =
  envelope group id, epoch threaded for rotation, D-16 nonce as the
  12-byte sealed-blob layout); the relay gains two opaque,
  bearer-gated, subject-scoped routes (PUT one's own agreement key, GET
  the account's set) plus schema v3; both shells bootstrap at sign-in
  (keypair → publish → receive-or-found) and gate pushLatest on an
  authority marker — a never-authorised device refuses to poison the
  shared log with self-keyed ciphertext. THE PROOF THAT REMOVED THE
  CRUTCH: two devices per shell, each with its OWN keypair and NO shared
  fixture secret, converge BECAUSE THE ENVELOPE PATH CARRIED THE KEY;
  fail-closed negatives (unauthorised restore throws, local ledger
  survives, recovers when authorised); GUARANTEES #7 over the relay's
  envelope bytes. Revocation wiring: a device removed from the envelope
  set receives nothing more. Sabotage: gate removed, authorise-to-self,
  founding marker unset — each red at the two-device proof; the iOS gate
  sabotage first PASSED (the 409-then-open-refusal path masked it) and
  the proof gained a tight anchor (no relay request at all) that then
  bit — recorded as the deviation it is. D-122-audit cleanups landed:
  iOS's dead prefix(4) u32FromBE deleted, 3-char canaries replaced with
  deterministic long tokens (the audit's 2^-24 correction), and a
  structural BUILD-LOG check joined the fast gate — which immediately
  caught D-93's duplicated row columns. Honest residue in §4.3: the
  lost-only-device question is the founder's open decision; two-key
  split on simultaneous founding; received-key retention until rotation.
  Full gate green on the committed tree (the working-tree run's only
  failure was bindings freshness against uncommitted work).

- **2026-09-07** — D-124: the six-word safety phrase, end to end, and the
  screens D-123 deferred. **SPEC A-01 had no coverage anywhere** while
  D-123's `authorise` wrapped the account's sync key to whatever
  agreement key the RELAY returned — and ADR-0021 designates the relay

  (§3.3's six words from a fixed 2048-word list, §12's approval screen)

  rotation); QR verification; key-change detection; and a first-class
  product entry point, which SPEC §12 asks for and which belongs to the
  account surface as a whole. Full gate 15/15 on the committed tree.

- **2026-09-07** — D-125: ADR-0034's second half. Sync is on by default

  style, not the (real, now fixed) missing AccentColor, but SwiftUI
  autolinking an email address in a string-literal title — and a new gate
  leg refuses the class. Also corrected in place: my own "13 + 5 executed"
  iOS tallies in D-126 and D-127, which were two class subtotals.

- **2026-09-14** — D-129: GUARANTEES #6 gains one exception. The founder
  decided Google Sign-In ships on both iOS and Android. #6 as written could
  not allow any Google or Apple sign-in, a conflict the CLAUDE.md verification
  pass had surfaced. It was amended before release and loudly — ADR-0035, a
  dated Amendments section in GUARANTEES.md, matching SPEC, README and
  THREAT_MODEL text — under seven binding constraints: explicit tap only;
  system sign-in surface only; the app's own requests to the relay alone, with
  a relay-issued nonce; `openid` only; no Google libraries outside the Android
  Play build; no linking identities by email; nothing else riding the
  exception. The founder also reported Play organisation verification and
  Apple developer verification complete.

- **2026-09-14** — D-130: Sign in with Google, relay side. Three routes: a
  single-use nonce the relay issues, Android's ID-token sign-in, and iOS's
  code exchange, which the relay performs so the app itself never talks to
  Google (ADR-0035). One audience per path, both of Google's issuer
  spellings, only `sub` consumed, the nonce spent before verification, and a
  relay with no client ids refuses everything. Apple and Google now share one
  key cache. Finding: D-63's key-rotation test could not fail — its cache was
  empty throughout — and is corrected. Sabotage 12/12, after my own runner
  mislabelled every red row as a compile error and was re-evaluated from its
  logs. Nothing has touched real Google yet; that needs the founder's OAuth
  client ids and a deploy.

- **2026-09-14** — D-131: Sign in with Apple gets the relay nonce. ADR-0035
  already required a single-use, relay-issued nonce for every ID token on both
  platforms; D-63's Apple path had none, so an Apple token could be replayed
  until it expired. The relay now issues Apple nonces from their own store,
  spends one before verifying, and refuses a token whose `nonce` claim is not
  the nonce presented with it. A request without a nonce gets the same uniform
  401 as every other failure. The iOS client fetches and sends the nonce; the
  buttons are D-132. Fixed before the founder's pending deploy, so it costs him
  no extra one. The unit's first full gate also caught RUSTSEC-2026-0285, a
  rustls advisory published that day, and rustls moved to 0.23.45 in the same
  commit, so D-130's commit must not be the one deployed.

- **2026-09-14** — D-132: Sign in with Apple on iOS, and the Google flow behind
  it. Apple's own button now sits at the top of Sign in, asks Apple for nothing
  but who you are, and carries the relay's single-use nonce. The Google flow
  (the system web sheet, PKCE, a checked state, scope `openid`, and the relay
  doing the code exchange) is built and tested, but its button stays hidden
  until there is a client id and Google's official mark. Two build failures on
  the way were mine: a truncated read of a project-file line, and an `await`
  inside a test assertion. Looking at the screen on the simulator found a stray
  hairline under the button, now gone. A tap against production gave the
  uniform rejection because production still runs code from before D-130.

- **2026-09-14** — D-133: Sign in with Google on Android, Play build only. The
  relay nonce, Credential Manager and Google's own sheet are wired, and the
  button stays hidden until there is a Web client id and a branding decision.
  The direct build carries no Google code, proven in the dex it ships (0 Google
  type names against the play build's 2,000-odd), not just in its Gradle file.
  A launch on an emulator without Google Play services showed nothing from
  Google running at start-up. On the way: the Play-manifest gate leg turned out
  to find its file by luck (never falsely, checked against the packaged APK)
  and is now pinned; `googleid` would have smuggled a beta into the app; every
  stable Credential Manager provider still pulls an alpha; Google's "G" mark
  already ships inside `play-services-auth`; and my own sabotage runner ran one
  variant per row until Gradle was told `--continue`.

- **2026-09-14** — D-134: groups and people, core half. Core can now mint a
  participant id and hold a member's name. A group with names always lists the
  same ids, in the same order, as the group the balance code reads. Names are
  trimmed, capped at 64 characters (not bytes), and free of control characters.
  Two other members cannot share a name, but you can share one with someone,
  because you will see yourself as "Tim (You)". The shells do not use it yet;
  that is D-135 and D-136. On the way my own bindings count read zero because of
  a grep quirk with a single file, and the regenerated bindings were staged
  before the full gate so the freshness check compared what is actually being
  committed.

- **2026-09-18** — D-135: groups and people on iOS. A fresh install now
  starts empty, with "Create a group", instead of a fixture trip, four
  fixture people and four fixture expenses. You give your name once and see
  yourself as "Tim (You)", and you can keep many groups, pick one, and add or
  rename people. A ledger from before names asks for your name and keeps
  every record: the founder's simulator ledger migrated with its balances
  unchanged. Looking at it found more: Settle recomputed from the fixtures
  after a settlement, iOS Balance ignored settlements, expense dates showed
  the minute (a D-54 typo), and a test had passed only because export seeded
  a group. My own draft also nearly erased every group on an unreadable list,
  and my S2 sabotage expectation was wrong, corrected and rerun. Xcode 27
  arrived mid-unit: the gate now picks the newest simulator, skips Xcode's
  10-minute failure diagnostics, and iOS 26+'s pill-shaped list rows are
  recorded as a trap.

- **2026-09-18** — D-136: groups and people on Android, the twin of D-135.
  On Android the first expense saved on a fresh install would have written
  the fixture Goa Trip, paid by the fixture Ada. That is gone: Android now
  starts empty with "Create a group", asks your name once, shows "Tim (You)",
  keeps many groups, and adds or renames people, with copy identical to iOS.
  Looking closer found two more defects: a failed settlement was silently
  dropped and left the button saying "Settling…" for good, and an import would
  have erased every stored name. Both are fixed and tested. On the emulator,
  an upgraded app kept its record after asking for a name, and a fresh
  install went from onboarding to a settled debt. One of my sabotage
  expectations was wrong again (A6), corrected and rerun.

- **2026-09-18** — D-137: gate speed. The founder asked why checks took over
  30 minutes. Measured: macOS assesses every new compiler plugin and test
  binary, and that, not the checks, is where the time goes. He enabled the
  Developer Tools exemption, but this unit found the scan still running in
  Claude's gates (191 assessments in 10 minutes; a fast gate of 20m37s), and
  reported it. What a script can fix is doing proven work twice. The
  pre-commit hook now runs the quick checks on every commit, and skips the
  slow Rust checks only when a clean gate already passed on exactly the staged
  inputs with the same toolchain. Before, a commit that touched only a check
  script, BUILD-LOG or Swift ran no check at all. Every gate leg is now timed.
  The gate's own self-test is a new leg (18 in all); sabotage 10/10. The relay
  runbook's three mistakes from the 2026-09-18 upgrade are fixed, with a new
  "Updating a running relay" section. D-135's five pointers to "D-137" for the
  iOS 27 work are corrected in place.

- **2026-09-18** — D-138: Sign in with Google goes live. The founder created
  the Google Cloud clients and approved Google's official button art, so the
  flows built in D-132 and D-133 are switched on. On iOS, Apple's and Google's
  buttons now sit together at one size; on Android, Google's button appears in
  the Play build only, and the F-Droid/GitHub build still carries nothing from
  Google (checked in the built app). Against the live relay, Google accepted
  SKIPTI's sign-in request on iOS ("Sign in to continue to SKIPTI"), and
  Android reached Google's own sheet. Finishing a sign-in needs the founder's
  own Google or Apple account. Found on the way: on Android 15 and later the
  app draws under the status bar, now its own task.

- **2026-09-19** — D-139: iOS 27 adoption. On iOS 26 and later, a button
  placed as a clear list row is cut into a pill, and five screens still had
  one: Add expense, Your name, New group, Sign in and Import review. Each
  screen's main action now sits in a bar under the form, the system's own
  place for it, and on Add expense it rides above the keyboard. The Balance
  account icon is pinned on iOS 27 so it can never be pushed into an
  overflow menu. Sync tests that used to time out now name the error they
  hit. A new gate check stops a button from being placed that way again.
  Checked on iOS 27 and on the founder's iOS 26.5 ledger.

- **2026-09-19** — D-140: the account icon is now on every tab, on iPhone and
  Android, not only on Balance. On the way, Android Studio had quietly

- **2026-09-21** — D-141: the groundwork for editing and deleting expenses.
  An edit is now its own record, applied field by field in the same order on
  every device, so two phones editing different things both keep their
  change, and two phones setting different amounts are asked which to keep
  instead of one silently winning. A delete can be undone. Both apps now
  build the ledger through the same code in the Rust core. Found and fixed on
  the way: an old one-time migration would have turned every edited expense
  into a duplicate on the next sync. The screens come next.

- **2026-09-21** — D-142: editing and deleting expenses on iPhone. Tap an
  expense on the Expenses tab to see the whole split and who added and last

  opening it. When two phones set different amounts, the expense says so and
  asks which to keep, as SPEC §6.1 requires. The list's header now reads
  "1 EXPENSE", not "EXPENSES · 1 RECORDS", and two expenses by the same payer
  no longer share an identity in the list. Android follows in D-143.

- **2026-09-21** — D-143: the same on Android. Tap an expense for its detail,
  then Edit or Delete (asked first, with Undo straight after); touch and hold

- **2026-09-21** — D-144: Settings, with an Appearance choice of System,
  Light, Dark or Night (a pure-black Dark for dark rooms and OLED screens),
  on both phones. Your data now has a home there: Export on both phones and

  shortcuts, so the promise that your data is exportable in one tap was not
  true in the app itself until now. Also fixed: switching from Night to Dark

- **2026-09-21** — D-145: your profile, on this device. Settings now opens

- **2026-09-21** — D-146: About. Settings now ends with About: the app and

- **2026-09-22** — D-148: the apps' monospaced font is now IBM Plex Mono

- **2026-09-22** — D-149: deleting a SKIPTI account now waits seven days.

- **2026-09-24** — D-150: you can delete your SKIPTI account from Settings

- **2026-09-24** — D-154: if you used SKIPTI on two devices before signing
